body: Very unethical please avoid! You sit on a podium watching a herd of 30 elephants, including babies, go and get fed some water/nutrients (unclear what it was). These elephants are shrieking constantly, which I have never heard before in other sanctuaries. They are hit by a man with a stick if they return for more food/water, then try and run and avoid him-all clearly petrified
title: AVOID- VERY SAD

body: I was very disappointed with my visit to the elephant sanctuary. This place is supposed to protect and care for baby elephants, but what I saw really upset me.Some staff members were beating the baby elephants to keep them calm. These are small animals, already separated from their mothers, and they need care and kindness, not force. It was painful to watch.This is no way to treat animals. Visitors come here thinking it's a safe place for elephants, but the behavior we witnessed was unacceptable.I hope management improves their practices, properly trains the staff, and treats these animals with more respect and care.I can't recommend this place until real changes occur.
title: Very Sad Experience – Not What We Expected

body: This is a home where they treat orphaned young elephants before they are released to the wild. For the short time we were there they seemed to be well looked after. You do need to get there at feeding time. It was lovely to see the elephants and know they will not be kept in captivity. There was an interesting information centre there too.
title: Seemed to be well cared for

body: Honestly disappointed with the experience. Firstly they were very clearly using cattle prods to control the elephants. While I can understand elephants being large and potentially dangerous, the use seemed excessive and if they do that in front of guests...what are they doing behind the scenes? Secondly the feeding seemed very poorly planned. They lay out food but allow elephants into the feeding area in batches. So the first elephants get to feast, but elephants allowed in later end up wandering around aimlessly because all the food is gone. Doesn't seem well organized for animal wellfare at all! Also as a visit, was terrible - I was expecting just a basic presentation of what the sactuary is about (history of place, objectives, how things are going etc) but there was zero communication with guests. Just sit there and watch elephants being fed in batches. Intermitted with noises of cattle prods being deployed. Based on what I've read this place is genuine about its care of animals, which is really hope is true. But they need to improve their treatment of animals and guests. I hope people continue to support but this place needs to do better.
title: Unfortunately disappointed

body: This was very unethical and an unpleasant experience. We saw the elephants at feeding time, and they were sprinting to get their milk, as if they were starving. Baby elephants should have 10L of milk a day, but I don’t think they got anywhere near that before being pushed away by other elephants or the staff. All the elephants were completely terrified by one of the staff members, who was hitting them with a stick. We also heard reports of an electric taser being used previously on the baby elephants, and from their reactions when this one man came near them, i could tell that he had hurt them before. If you care about animals, please do not visit this place and give them money. I did not enjoy watching the animal abuse here, and would not recommend it.
title: UNETHICAL “SANCTUARY” - PLEASE AVOID!!

body: We were fortunate enough to visit the elephant transit home as part of a 3 week tour of Sri Lanka and it is another fabulous example of how Sri Lanka values and cares for its animals. The orphaned elephants appear to be well cared for and looked after, judging by their personalities and comic antics at feeding time. Well worth a visit if you are visiting Udawalawe National Park, or just near the area.
title: Beautiful orphan baby elephants being well cared for

body: We had Asan as our guide. He was very knowledgeable and spotted water buffalo deer elephants and crocodiles and many species of birds on our safari. He has worked in the park for about 35 years and knew so much about it. He was a very considerate driver and respectful of our ages and did not drive too fast. We highly recommend him. First class day all round!
title: Excellent day on safari

body: Don't go! They used electric tazors on the baby elephants for no reason and they scream in fear/pain! I left when I saw this i found it so upsetting, completely unnecessary nowadays. They are all nervous and avoid the man with the tazor - really sad and shocking from a centre that advocates welfare - pass! No photos just a video i will be passing on.
title: Electric shock baby elephants :( Pass!

body: This visit was an extremely disturbing experience.During feeding, we saw elephants being beaten by staff to force them to move forward. The animals seemed stressed, submissive and clearly constrained. Faced with this scene, we left the scene before the end.Regardless of the official discourse on rehabilitation, hitting elephants is not ethical and has no place in a center that claims to be a protector of animal welfare. The use of fear and physical coercion, especially in front of visitors, is totally incompatible with a care or rehabilitation approach.This tour is more like a tourist attraction in disguise than a respectful sanctuary. We left with deep discomfort and great sadness.I strongly advise against this experience to anyone sensitive to the animal cause or looking for a truly ethical approach.
title: To avoid

body: Just a magical experiance. Be aware - this isn’t a tourist trapYou won’t touch the elephantsYou won’t feed them You won’t wash themThis is a rehabilitation sanctuary. You will see them fed and it’s just fantastic. Around 40-50 elephants of all ages Get there 20 mins before the start for a good seating view. Wonderful !
title: A memorable experience

body: We have been here to see how the elephants are fed. They are taken care of here if they are injured or we are and are prepared to return to nature. You can see the times on the internet in advance when feeding is taking place and you can watch this from a grandstand to get the animals used to humans as little as possible but it is really nice to see the elephants running in groups to the milk. You can really see enough and it's worth it
title: Beautiful to see

body: This is a must do. Unlike the tourist trap of another place we visited, this one is doing it well for the right reasons. Didn’t see any of the criticised behaviours a couple of other reviewers commented on. Next day we even saw some of the rehabilitated and released elephants in the national park.So, just our experience :)
title: Fantastic, looks caring and ethical

body: I was happy I thought I was going to a sanctuary for abandoned baby elephants. Then I thought, how are there so many baby elephants? I truly hope they are released to wild herds. I left when the handler hit a baby right across the eye and hard on the back. Hit a few others too that were scared. Elephants dont forget and this would make them aggressive in the wild. :(
title: Elephant transit home

body: It was very impressive to see how the elephant babies are fed. Very entertaining and a great thing. Also the museum with lots of exciting information is recommended
title: Impressive number of elephant babies

body: They beat the animals with wooden sticks and you can see how the baby elephants are afraid of the handlers. Horrible experience.
title: Don't go.

body: If you come to Udawalawe, the best place to go is to see the beautiful baby elephants that are the most beautiful and healing... This place, which is very easily maintained by the Wildlife Department of the Sri Lankan government, is beautiful. These precious elephants were released back into the forest park after they reached the right age. The elephants came to the police station and drank milk, which was very beautiful. If you also come to Udawalawe, do not miss this place.
title: Beautiful Baby Elephant - Udawalawe

body: We visited this site early afternoon, it was very interesting to see. You can't feed the animals yourself, but you can see them up close. In addition, there is a small museum that explains species, evolution and the risk of extinction, it is really well done. The price is quite affordable, it would be a shame to miss out if you are around.
title: Nice experience

body: Got here just at breakfast time for the elephants. It's was just magical watching them take it in turns to go and get the milk before heading off to the other parts of there breakfast. The little one are so adorable and it's good to see them playing with each other
title: Fantastic place to watch the elephants

body: If you do nothing else in Sri Lanka, you must do this! We couldn't stop smiling! A wonderful sight and a great cause as the aim is to return every elephant to the wild.
title: A Must See Experience

body: ⚠️⚠️ANIMAL ABUSERS⚠️⚠️THEY BEAT THE ELEPHANTS AND TASER THEM WITH ELECTRIC TASERS. This is one of the most unethical "sanctuaries" I have ever seen. The “transit home” is set up to look like they care about the elephants and treat them kindly. But this couldn’t be further from the truth. It is a money making scheme under the guise of a “rescue”. If you care about animals at all, please do not visit this place. I spoke to the reception staff about this to which I received no reply, just laughing. A horrific hell on earth for elephants.
title: ANIMAL ABUSERS

body: So cute! There were maybe 30 elephants today; mostly babies, but some older ones. The whole process took about 25 minutes - so don't be late 😊
title: Cute - Makes you want to cuddle them!

body: This is a real release project, quite unlike the so-called Elephant Orphangage in Kegalle. Here the babies are left to roam freely in the national park during the day, but they get the necessary milk twice/d for about 5 years. So that they don't get too used to people, you can watch them, but only from a greater distance, there is no touching at all. It's the largest orphaned baby elephant release project in the world, a good thing.
title: One good thing: the largest release project for orphaned elephant babies worldwide

body: Super nice experience, educational info center and the way the orphans are helped is wonderful to see. With great respect and as few human contacts as possible. A great initiative!
title: Ethical and responsible

body: This was an interesting way to pass an hour if it's on your way. A little chaotic as it was weekend and there were a lot of locals there too. Our guide suggested we looked round an information area first which provided alot of information on Elephants. Not so much about what they do here but interesting all the same. It was lovely to see the babies feeding close up and it reassuring to know they will be released back into the wild.
title: Worth a look

body: Great for adults and children alike. Feeding time is controlled but hilarious as you see c60 young elephants feed milk and bamboo.Only lasts about half an hour but given the great job they’re doing it’s just lovely to know most of these orphaned/ injured youngsters will be re-released back into the national in the future
title: Time to smile….but a hugely worthwhile project

body: There are 3 feeding times a day when tourists can go and watch the elephants come out to be fed which we didn’t realise until we arrived. It was lovely seeing all the baby elephants and how they are fed milk (through a tube). Having some information/ commentary would be good while the elephants are feeding so we can understand more on how these elephants got to be in this establishment in the first place/ their names etc. At present it just felt like a tourist attraction rather than an elephant rehabilitation centre, it was very busy. As we’d just seen elephants in the wild in Udawalawe which was magical, we could have missed this in hindsight as it didn’t feel as special.
title: Nice to see but definitely just a busy tourist attraction

body: Always I was selecte elphant transit home in Udawalawe for my forieng clients .it's very worth to my clients & they enjoy & satisfied even the resanable enterance tickets price too .guests are more like milk feeding moments Thanks Best journey holiday tours
title: Udawalawe elphant transit home

body: Experience not appreciated. The place opens just before the supply of food to the elephants. Lots of people, chaos and confusion. Elephants only seem to be a tourist attraction and the usefulness of the rehabilitation centre is not valued. Nice museum inside. Regarding the use of the electric stick I think it's a debated ethical issue. For my part, I understand the need for regulation on food and space, but perhaps other ways of managing these variables could be found. I did not fully understand the usefulness of the place because it is not explained. You're just left there to watch so many little elephants bingeing and fighting over food. It's not worth going.
title: Better the Safari

body: A really nice place to visit, even with children. No matter where you choose to settle, there is good view for the elephants, and it is clear that the animals thrive and are well taken care of. The small museum is definitely worth a visit, as is the area around the square – there is plenty to see and experience.Good advice: Make sure to devote plenty of time to the whole experience. Unfortunately, our driver had not planned enough time, so we had to hurry up and miss some of the details.All in all an experience we can warmly recommend!
title: Worth a visit

body: After reading several reviews of elephant orphanages and the bad press of “Pinnawala”I wanted to visit a place that was less touristy and had more of the animals welfare at the forefront.The ETH facility is set up very well to educate the visitors and you can tell that money has been invested to encourage people to visit but that’s it really.I could see the elephants were getting frustrated at being penned up against a gate prior to feeding time (which was running late)and I was not impressed with the overuse of the electrical baton by one particular keeper to maintain control up to the milk feeding station causing the calve to moan loudly.It raises the question as to whether these elephants are rehabilitated to go back into the wild or it’s just a tourist attraction as there’s no info or stats on release figures anywhere.I think one day the elephants will turn on the keepers as they never forget!
title: Educational experience marred by overuse of electrical baton on elephants making them cry out!

body: We visited in an evening having undertaken an early morning safari. Was very well organised. Worth remembering that you're essentially visiting a charity or NPO that allows visitors in to help fund their work. Was absolutely brilliant, they were all fed within 20 ish minutes. Was so funny to observed the behaviour & greediness of some of the elephants. Having read some other reviews we were a bit concerned animals might be being exploited, but this really didn't seem to be the case at all. Certainly a brief experience to add onto your visit to Udawalawe, but well worth dropping in.
title: Absolutely brilliant experience

body: Great to see the baby & adult elephants at feeding time.Such characters xAppear well cared for & healthy.Perfect experience for children x
title: Great experience ❤️

body: First to clarify (as we couldn’t get a clear answer online), feeding times are 10:30am, 2 and 6pm. We didn’t know what to expect and this was a terrific experience. It was adorable to watch the little ones and the fascinating to watch the bigger ones. We probably saw about 60 while we were there. Even a larger elephant with a prosthetic who was apparently injured during the war. We stayed way after everyone left it was that good. So too was the educational center
title: Could’ve stayed all day!

body: Very nice if you take care of the elephants and feed them.However, with the electric baton scare away at the milk feeding station until they make strange noises we do not think okay.
title: Show 3x Daily

body: I was there, after 20 minutes I had to leave. 2 men fed and sent 3 elephants for milk. Why didn't they let only 2 elephants go when they fed 2 people. The third elephant demanded food and so that he wouldn't disturb them they hit him with an electric gun until the little elephant cried.. Children don't understand this. and this behavior is inappropriate.. a man ran among the elephants and scared them with electricity, when he didn't listen he got a shock.. terrible and people pay for it. I wish the same to the man who has this position.
title: I was there, after 20 minutes I had to leave. 2 men fed and sent 3 elephants for milk. Why didn't they let only 2 elephants go w

body: RUN AWAY!I don’t understand how they have 4.5/5.There are at least 50 elephants of all ages... where do they come from? How did they get there? How are they released? Where do they sleep? No explanation!They are released 3 by 3... there are at least 150 tourists watching them on a bleacher so full of noise = a lot of stress.They are fed for 30 seconds and then beaten to go and eat leaves (which are insufficient for the number of elephants and not enough trees to go and feed themselves)Knowing that a mother elephants has a gestation of 22 months and that an adult elephant needs 150kg of food.. I don't see how they can be released into the wild afterwards.We were fooled by their message of hope but please do not make the same mistake.
title: Run away!

body: We had a lovely time watching the young elephants, being fed and nurtured in order for them to be released into the vast nature reserve surrounding the elephant transit home Despite all their attention, the elephants are given the least amount of human contact so that their release into the wild will be more natural
title: Kids will love this one

body: This is a great experience and they are doing a great job nursing orphaned elephants back to the wild. A must do experience.
title: Elephant Transit Home

body: Worthwhile stop at Elephant Transit Home in Udawale. Very nice to see that people are taking care of the orphaned elephant here. You can see them up close, there is a very well done Visitors Center on the premises. No stupid tourists - Nepp - promotions, fair entrance fee (5,50 EUR), you see elephants up close and learn a lot about them...
title: Great collection station with elephants up close, visitors center and no tourists - Nepp

body: We really enjoyed the opportunity to see and learn more about this project and the work that it does to help elephants transition back to the wild. Some other reviews make reference to the calves being mistreated - we did not see any such treatment during our visit. The calves looked happy, well nourished and full of energy and the caretakers appeared to be taking good care of their charges.
title: Feeding Time for the Elephant Calves!

body: Absolutely amazed by this experience ! Wonderful to see the baby elephants feeding on their milk then leaves .Some really little ones … so sweet .so glad they are being looked after so well .Loved it. Thoroughly recommend.
title: Great experience

body: The Elephant Transit Home (ETH) in Udawalawe is a must-visit for wildlife lovers. Unlike traditional elephant orphanages, ETH focuses on rehabilitating orphaned elephant calves and preparing them for release back into the wild. Visitors can observe the elephants during feeding times from a viewing platform, ensuring minimal human interaction to support their reintegration into nature. The center is well-managed and plays a crucial role in Sri Lanka’s conservation efforts. A visit here offers an educational and ethical wildlife experience.
title: Elephant Transit Home Udawalawe: A Heartwarming Conservation Experience

body: Such a lovely place. We loved the whole experience of watching the Elephant's feeding time. They were adorable. The ethos of the place was good and the small exhibition was interesting
title: Adorable Elephants

body: Local people confirmed to me that the elephants are only kept for profit reasons, not for their protection. The same goes for turtle hatcheries. So if you care about animals, please consider skipping these types of tourist entertainment.
title: Making money on the expense of animals

body: You oay to watch elephants being fed as part of the rehabilitation process.I assume monet taken on the gate, which isn't much goes to the program
title: Visit if you're in town

body: Great trip out. Very informative and interesting. Jeep safari is a must brilliant day out, lots to see even an elephant that has false leg lives there. Cared for very well
title: Elephant orphanage

body: Please please please DO NOT support this! We, like most people thought it sounded wonderful - a sanctuary for orphaned elephants who would one day be released into the wild again. The elephants we saw were young (I would question how they had quite so many babies) and were visibly terrified of the keeper who had a stick he was hitting them with. Read that again, hitting baby elephants. We were told it was to make sure they feared humans. I have never seen this before in any kind of sanctuary. There was no necessity for him to even be in the pen with them. It is a tourist trap, pure and simple. I would not be surprised if the elephants were kept hungry before the ‘feeding times’ as well - I’ve never seen baby elephants in the wild run for milk like these did. It is sad and needs a complete overhaul or to be closed. There is no space for cruelty in something which claims to be doing good.
title: Cruel to elephants - do not visit

body: The elephants are fed by humans and thus become accustomed to human contact. After release in wildlife parks, this can therefore lead to problems: which already happens here and there!
title: Questions remain

body: Please don't go there if you love animals and you care about elephants! The little ones were just beaten violently with sticks and also shocked with electric sticks from the beginning for no reason. You could see how scared the little babies were and you could hear their cries. I thought it was so cruel that I just had to leave.
title: Please don't go

body: absolutely beautiful place full of the cutest baby elephants, who can throw a tantrum like any moody toddler and are so funny to hear how demanding they can get when the milk is taken awaythese elephants are hopefully going to be released into the wild so human interaction is limited but you can see how loved they are and how well cared for and they live with a great deal of space and stunning scenery to roam around inthere is a lovely museum attached that you can visit after the feeding and gain a lot of knowledge about elephants and their needs and the shop although small has some lovely gifts at reasonable prices
title: a beautiful experience

body: People go there and donate. This is a shelter that wants the orphans between the ages of 5 and 7 back in the wild. So you have no contact with the elephants here you can watch them get food per 3 in the stands. That's the idea but it goes wrong sometimes which is a very nice sight. There is also a shop selling stuff made by fellow villagers and there is a very nice museum that explains everything about the elephant.
title: Highly recommended

body: A visit absolutely to do whether you are with children or just between adults. Seeing elephants eating leaves and drinking milk from huge bottles is really very cute and funny. Of course you go because in the safari area so you will not waste time to reach the place and you will enjoy their first daily meal.
title: Transit house of elephants

body: What beautiful animals these are. We enjoyed this special visit. Although, of course, these are young elephants that are orphans. This project gives them a chance to live in the wild. The animals get a portion of milk, the little ones a bit more. But they are supposed to learn to live in the wild. Too bad some people come here and apparently don't understand. Yes the animals are coached and sometimes reprimanded, like today a young bull who wanted extra milk and pushed other animals away. The staff handled that well, but clearly. They must be wild animals, after all. The goal is to allow the elephant to live independently in the wild again. That's where the training was founded. Keep that in mind and you will have the chance to see these mighty animals up close.
title: Powerful creature, in training for return to the wild.

body: This could be a wonderful place for elephants, and the signs explaining why they use sticks make you believe it is, but after watching the staff with the elephants for 30 minutes at feeding time we all came away traumatised. The elephants are hit really hard with sticks, and often for no reason at all. We saw elephants just standing there doing nothing at all and being hit and kicked! Some of the sticks were used as weapons, jabbing the elephants in the head and legs. The staff did not come across as friendly or kind. My daughter loves elephants and came away heartbroken.
title: Great cause but with cruelty

body: Just wow! If you like elephants you must visit! Wonderful experience; our children loved it. Great. Museum onsite interesting too. Thank you.
title: Just wow!

body: DO NOT GO!! This place is NOT ethical, visibly beating the elephants, restricting food, pulling their tails. Couldn’t stay for more than 2 minutes without getting upset. Please please please do not give these horrible people your money
title: Animal abuse awful

body: I find this facility difficult to review as we are being told that elephants are being cared for and returned to the wild but the whole experience we saw seems very artificial. The use of the sticks by the keeper seemed excessive and the elephants were visibly afraid of them.
title: Not for me

body: I don’t usually write reviews but i was SO disappointed by this experience that I left five minutes in. This is supposedly an ‘animal protection organisation’ however this is not what I saw at all during my visit. At first it seems all cute as a lot of baby elephants come out but soon after a man with a white stick comes out and starts hitting the elephants WITH force, and the elephants are crying because of this. This is not ethical and I don’t see how this prepares them to live back in the wild. I have been to an elephant sanctuary before where the elephants are cared for by local families, free to roam, well fed, hydrated and bathed and minimal human interaction. Elephants at this transit home do not seem to be treated well and it seems to be more for the entertainment of visitors. I am so disappointed and angered at this treatment and lack of transparency. Do not declare yourself an animal protection organisation yet abuse animals to do what you want them to do.
title: Not an animal protection organisation

body: One and only place to observe baby elephants. This transit home is taking care a lot of orphan elephant babies until they can survive theirselves. Staff are doing very good job. They feed baby elephants with milk three times per day. 10.30, 2.30 and 6.30. Both 10.30 and 2.30 feeding times are allowed for visitors. You can enter the premises after buying a tickets and counter will be open 30min before the show. There is a detailed elephant museum too. Also they provide good toilet facility too. There are enough parking space any size of vehicle. Only drawbacks were I noticed are there isn't any proper waiting space for early visitors and there aren't proper seat for visitors at show pavilion. Seating in cement floor while will comeup with back pain.
title: Lost in paradise of elephant babies

body: I am torn. If it is really true that orphaned elephants are cared for here and released back into the wild, it is somewhat justifiable. I was still shocked at how the animals were treated. If they did not do what the ETH employees wanted, they were beaten quite violently with sticks or pulled on their trunks and tails. I find these methods very questionable. In my opinion, the animals did not have a good opinion of the employees there and there seems to be a reason for that. I would not visit again and would be in favor of a professional, independent inspection by international animal rights activists.
title: Does it really serve animal welfare? Questionable institution

body: Explore the rich biodiversity of Udawalawa National Park. Keep your eyes peeled for leopards, sloth bears, crocodiles, and a variety of bird species
title: Udawalawa National Park

body: It's horrible. Just awful. It's a real business without a name. We pay a lot to see baby elephants stolen from their mothers, yes stolen. It is a myth that these babies were abandoned. Elephants in Udawalawe Park live safely. There are no poachers and mothers do not abandon their young. On the other hand, this false "orphana" organized to collect the babies and make a circus for the tourists, there were around 50 to 60 babies. It's impossible that so many babies were abandoned, they just say that to make people swallow the pill. The truth is, tourists love seeing babies up close. They built an arena. They open the doors 3 times a day, each time there are between 100 and 200 tourists. They earn around 40,000 euros per month, which is huge for Sri Lanka.It’s an extremely well-crafted business.In the country we find the same thing with turtle sanctuaries...Please don't feed these businesses.
title: Horrible. Sad.

body: A wonderful project helping orphan elephants. Great explanations around how they minimise the disruption to the elephants life, as well as promoting as quickly and swiftly as possible, their freedom back to the wild.
title: A great hope for a wonderful animal!

body: I wanted to go to the elephant transit home for so many years as many years ago I used to sponsor elephants from here. I thought I’d be able to do more here and get closer to the elephants, but that wasn’t the case, and once it was explained to me, it made perfect sense! It was still lovely to see the elephants being fed. They are so cute.
title: Don’t miss this

body: Wonderful to see orphaned baby elephants being cared for. Definitely worth a visit. Excellent value.Would highly recommend.
title: Great place to see baby elephants

body: We were booked in to this sanctuary as part of a Mercury holidays tour of Sri Lanka holiday. We arrived on time for the “ show” of feeding time in the morning. Visitors sit in a tiered viewing area and watch the elephants gather for feeding. We saw approximately 50 elephants, youngest being about a month old. Takes about half hour. The elephants get rehabilitated back in the wild once they’re old enough and paired up. Some who are poorly stay. They’re doing a good job, I’d have liked the opportunity to maybe get closer and what would help them raise money would be a shop! - our tour group would definitely have bought gifts if it helped the baby elephants, but nothing there.
title: Came as part of a tour group

body: We were there during feeding time. Adorable to see the baby elephants that come running to get milk from the handlers. Go early to get a good seat,
title: Wonderful Nature Resort - Elephants

body: The "home" looks after orphan elephants, the aim being to reintroduce them into the wild.We watched one of the twice daily feeding sessions. Excellent display of their work, and a great way to raise funds. (Get there reasonably early to get a central seat)
title: Very entertaining, well put together (plus "cute baby Elephants !)

body: Says open all day from 8am but won't let us in til the feeding times tried to call before no one picks up now waiting round for hours
title: Not as advertised

body: Had a lovely couple of hours watching the elephants be fed. They seem to do a great job rehabilitating the elephants and then returning them to the wild.
title: Nice experience

body: What a wonderful experience, watching these baby elephants arrive for their milk and I applaud the concept that we can watch from a distance but not get close to these wild animals. There was a sign explaining why they use sticks and we didn’t see overuse of these. There are many elephants in a small area and some of the bigger ones try to get more than their fair share of milk and can get a little bit pushy to the smaller ones. Some of them were only months old…gorgeous!
title: Not to be missed

body: Not happy about the whipping! The elephants are quite clearly scared of the workers who use a cane to whip them when they come back for more Milk. We saw elephants been hit in the face and body. I understand they need to keep control of them as there is a lot of Elephants but it’s was horrible to watch when you thought you were going to an orphanage/ elephant sanctuary. I really hope that the elephants are been looked after and not just used for monetary gain here …..
title: Need to stop the whipping

body: We visited with some trepidation and expectation as to some of the negative reviews. However our experience showed a well run sanctuary with animals in the best of condition. Feeding time was incredibly entertaining and the staff were most attentive to the "rowdy" adoloscents.Reccomend a visit to support a valuable resource.
title: Young elephants well cared for

body: Elephants are hit on their trunks if they are too pushy when feeding. So you regularly hear elephants protesting. Sometimes beaten with sticks. How do they get so many elephants? So a bit dubious. I don't recommend supporting this by watching.
title: Do not!

body: This so-called sanctuary tortured its animals. Baby elephants are stung at the joints of the hind legs, the hindquarters and the trunk when they do not make room quickly enough for others who come to drink their milk. Even more shocking, only one man arrives and all the baby elephants leave immediately without the latter making the slightest gesture.We went to express our disapproval. The answer was that it was necessary for the elephant to be afraid of humans so as not to damage the crops once released.This therefore confirms the fact that they are hitting them. We told them that it cannot be described as a sanctuary but as a business. Neither the man nor the elephant comes into play because if it was a question of preserving man and his cultures why then save the baby elephants.Do not give them your money which has no other purpose than to make them earn money by lying about their motivation.
title: Fire pump but certainly not a sanctuary

body: I read several reviews before going along, and I did not see any cruelty, only love and understanding as the young elephants develop relationships and growth. It was very moving, and I would recommend a visit.
title: Relationships and growth in observation

body: I urge you not to visit this ‘sanctuary’ if you care about animals and their welfare. We visited ETH a few days ago on recommendation from our tour company and were disgusted with the abuse we saw- staff members brutally whipping the elephants in the face, head, ribs and feet with full force. There are many other reviews citing the same type of abuse and even twisting and pulling the elephants tails and trunks. The elephants are visibly scared of the staff members and show physical fear and flinching when they are approached by the staff. I dread to think what goes on behind the scenes when these beatings are happening in plain sight. Many people have walked out of this place within a few minutes after seeing the horrific animal treatment. If you want to see elephants young and old I would recommend going on safari and seeing them free from abuse in their natural habitat. I hope that people will continue to report the abuse they see at this facility so that a change can happen. Appalled at what I have seen.
title: ANIMAL ABUSE

body: Such a special experience watching the orphaned baby elephants being fed. The adjoining restaurant is extremely pricey and food is below average.
title: Orphaned baby elephants

body: Pleasant time spent seeing a large number of baby elephants feeding. They are probably well taken care of and we did not observe any particular violence despite the presence of sticks held by the employees. Too bad the museum was closed.
title: Pleasant to observe

body: Do NOT come here, this place is not ethical at all. At first everything seemed okay, after a few minutes the elephants were repeatedly hit for wanting more food which is an instinctual behaviour. The way they were treated was horrible to the point that we had to walk out after around 5-10 minutes. Please do not support this place by giving them money to visit.
title: NOT ethical

body: Would NOT recommend, this place was definitely not ethical, the way they were treating the elephants was awful. Had to walk out half way through! DO NOT GO HERE
title: STAY WELL CLEAR - VERY UNETHICAL

body: What a brilliant experience to see all the baby and juvenile elephants come trotting in to be fed. And then watch as the cheeky ones try to come back for seconds. There are two or three feeds a day so plenty of flexibility for you can visit. But whichever feed you go to, best to get there early as there is no reserved seating. In fact it's just standing on terraces.
title: Elephant, elephant, elephant!!!

body: We visited as part of a trip, there was a big group of us and could only bear watching for part of the feeding. Whilst understanding that the home only has a certain amount of food for each elephant. The way the elephants were treated was appalling, they were hit with sticks, hit in the face and their tails twisted and pulled. It was complete abuse. Until the ETH improves this completely unnecessary treatment, I would avoid visiting.
title: Elephant abuse which needs to change

body: The work that is done here is very good. It is clear that the elephants are cared for well but the main priority is to return them to their natural habitat and way of life. This is sustainable tourism. Highly recommend visiting if you want an elephant experience that is good for the elephants.
title: Sustainable tourism must see!

body: Very nice moment with these Baby’s, some of them very funny! Indeed we learn nothing there but let's have a great time!
title: Very nice !

body: Having read some of the reviews on this site we were unsure about visiting. We are so very glad we did. What they are doing here is wonderful to see- watching the young elephants come running in to be fed is a joyous sight. Yes, they do use sticks to manage the elephants. There is a notice explaining why they use the sticks and it is clear to see why there is a need when the elephants try to beat the system. Feeding around 50 young elephants by hand is not an easy task and this is how they manage it to ensure each one is fed it’s share. We loved our visit and would encourage others to visit, by visiting you are supporting the rescue and rehabilitation of these beautiful creatures before they are released back into the wild.
title: Go, it is a joyous experience

body: Elephant calf recovery area. We arrived before 10:30 and you see how they give the little babies milk to drink. It lasts approximately 30 minutes and costs about 5 euros per person.
title: Curious

body: This Transit Home is a state facility that is also supported by German zoos (for example, Cologne Zoo donates GPS collars), which is why we assume that the elephants are really being released into the wild there.We thought it was good that the elephants were not paraded and were kept at a certain distance from people, so they were not putting on some kind of show.Yes, two men had sticks, but since these two were in the herd to let the elephants take turns drinking, this is justified in my opinion. No elephants were hit/stung "just like that".There is a small "museum" for this.
title: Very interesting

body: I visited here end of June 23 and I have to say this has been a highlight for my trip to Sri Lanka. We all know about the vulnerability of elephants in the wild and it was such a positive experience to visit a genuine sanctuary who take in young elephants from around Sri Lanka and rehabilitate them to be released into the wild. It was a joy to watch them at feeding time (we went for 6pm feeding time) and to see all their different personalities etc. You cannot touch or feed the elephants - this is to minimise human contact to aid their rehabilitation. Pleas donate whilst you’re there is you can- I believe the elephants have around 4 x milk packages a day and the sanctuary rely on donations.
title: Transit home Udawalawe

body: I agree with other reviewers on many things,The elephants were allowed into an enclosure 2 or 3 at a time to get fed milk whilst we sat on benches and watched. There were 2 men beating a little baby elephant with a stick just because it was a little over zealous at feeding time and other elephants I witnessed being hit. After they were fed the milk they munched on the grass whilst more elephants were led in 2 or 3 at a time. The process lasted no more than 30 minutes or so then the elephants were led back out. Not what I expected and wouldn’t recommend.
title: Would not recommend

body: I wasn’t totally sure about this place. It felt like a zoo and parade for the people. The babies are cute but I worry why so many there . Not totally sure how legitimate it is. Our guide suggested we go but in hindsight having been to Elephant Freedom and Minneriya National Park I would not of gone.
title: Unsure of legitimacy

body: We all agreed that our visit here was one of the most memorable parts of our Sri Lanka tour. Orphaned and rejected baby elephants come here and are looked after until they are ready to be released back into the wild. Make sure you time your visit for feeding time. It’s quite the spectacle !!
title: One of the highlights of our tour

body: I don' t know how I should rate this kind of experience because of the man with the stick. He hit the young elefants hard with this stick when they "misbehaved" and you could see that the elefants were afraid of his stick. The rest of the stuff loughed when he threatened the animals. I could hardly look at this and all the pleasure when I have seen the babies coming for food disappeared.On the other side this center is the only one that doesn't chain the elefants at night, as I read. They can walk around the area free. The work they do is acutally a good one but some things have to be improved. Because of this, I gave the second star. In Thailand we have visited a center much better than this, without cruelty towards the animals. But also there you have to inform yourself about the place you want to go to.
title: Mixed feelings about this place.

body: It is a nice little elephant sanctuary, but it is pricy based on the fact you only see the baby elephants from a distance for around 20-30mins then that’s it. Time to leave.Unsure if this was tour operator driven or this is how the park is,If coming here I would recommend doing as park of a safari or other things booked as it’s along way to travel (based on where your staying) for a 20/30min “show”
title: Short and sweet but expensive for a 30min show

body: Great place to visit and see numerous orphaned baby elephants. Unfortunately, there isn't a lot of information on offer or anyone to interact with. Head straight to the viewing platform to secure a good position and enjoy watching babies of all sizes feed. We went for the 2.30pm feeding time and stayed for about half an hour.
title: Baby elephants!

body: We called at this centre before before our safari. It was great to see the work they are doing at this centre to look at the orphan elephant that are rescued from the wild. The 20 minute feeding is a fun time that is all behind a serious project
title: An interesting place to visit to see the orphan elephants

body: A nice feel good experience watching the baby elephants get fed. Firstly, milk then after having their fill, head towards some sugar cane/maize plant/greenery :) Good to be able to observe their antics. The area of observation is concrete step seating and the babies are out "on show" for about 30minutes. It would make for a better understanding of how the transit home was run and how the orphans were rescued and released if there was a person or volunteer talking/commentating. However, there were many information boards with explanations. They mention some good success rate on release so it was quite heartening to see.
title: Baby elephants feeding time

body: We really enjoyed the time in Elephant’s transit home. 30 minutes of feeding baby elephants was very interesting and funny.
title: Baby elephant’s feeding

body: Baby elephants came running to get their milk quota. It was fun to watch how some of this tiny new born come running with big noise.
title: life time experience

body: This was one of the cutest experiences I've every had. Quite close to the baby elephants, running to get their milk. Can highly recommend it, such a heart-warming experience
title: Cutest elephants ever

body: This is a really great place to visit, but only during feeding time 2:30 -3:00 daily. About 50 or so elephants under 5 years old are fed a milk mixture and then some sugar cane, close to an observation area.The centre has a 100% success rate in returning elephants to the wild and you support halls them.
title: Excellent half hour visit

body: This home is filled with these little cuties. They play around and you get to see them eat, feed by the caretakers. Baby elephants are so extraordinary and to see them so close is an amazing experience. 🐘🐘
title: Little Cuties

body: A friend of mine recommended me to contact Lahiru for a tour in the Nationalpark and we were not disappointed. Lahiru was the best guide we could imagine for our safari. Everything was perfectly organised from beginning to end.It is incredible how he can spot even the smallest animals from a distance - i still don't know how he does it. Even though he knows a lot about the animals, he gives you time to enjoy and "inhale" the experience and silence.We took paths in which we almost never crossed other jeeps.He was respecting the moods of the animals and never pushed too hard. Like that, we saw a ton lot of animals from very close. Wow, I'm still stunned by the experience!Strong recommendation!
title: Amazing safari!

body: This place is supposed to be a successful rehab programme however we witnessed elephants being hit with sticks. The elephants are scared of the people supposedly looking after them. Would not recommend supporting this place.
title: Don't support this place

body: Great safari, we have seen many elephants. Lahiru was very punctual, brought us breakfast and we were always on paths that were not traveled by many truks. All around a super nice safari:) Thank you Lahiru!
title: Safari with good explanations and a relaxed atmosphere

body: For anyone who wishes to see baby elephants have a good time this is the place to visit. We stopped over at the afternoon feeding time and were entranced as these gorgeous youngsters came running in to get their milk. This is a must for any tourist who cares about wildlife and please remember to make a donation.
title: Wonderfully uplifting

body: So you see them in the wild on safari seemed only right to see these elephants as they are prepared for a life in the safari park once ready. You watch the feed essentially, no commentary or interaction with the elephants but you get plenty of entertainment! Was just the most amazing experience. Really helped complete our safari experience! Would highly recommend doing the two together!
title: A beautiful experience elephants just being looked after!

body: I actually had little idea of what I was getting into as I headed to the transit home because I had not really read up on the place before getting there, and what a lovely surprise it was! Lots of cute baby elephants on parade for us to see!Well actually you get in to see them during their feeding time. The evening time was from 18:00 entry. There is a viewing seating area from where we can watch the baby elephants being brought in groups of 3-4 at a time to get to their "milk station". It is so cute to see them racing to get to the milk. The milk is fed to them via a tube. The spectacle lasts quite a long time as there are many baby elephants..60+! I went there on a public holiday and it was full of local families with their children smiling and laughing at some of the baby elephant antics! It was a shame there was no one to explain to us about these elephants and how they got there, and give us any other info which would have made the visit even more interesting. But despite that I still highly recommend it! Not to mention the money spent (500 rupees) is a great contribution towards taking care of the elephants.
title: Adorable baby elephants! Must see!

body: Lahiru was a wonderful guide for our three hour safari. He is so knowledgeable with bundles of enthusiasm and an eye like a hawk. He spotted eagles, kingfishers, bee eaters, crocodiles and a well-camouflaged vine snake but the real thrill was his understanding of the elephants. He does not follow the other jeeps around but trusts his instincts to find the elephants and observe them close up. We had a bull elephant washing himself just a few feet away from our jeep, a juvenile trying to poke his trunk in to see what we were about and then our grand finale was the family he found just before leaving. Lahiru took some great photos for us too. His driver was fantastic and negotiated his way through the mud so well. Lahiru was good company, funny and informative but he also gave us time and space to enjoy the animals on our own. We could not recommend him more- he made our safari an absolute highlight of our Sri Lanka holiday.
title: Lahiru - a great guide

body: It was great to watch the 40+ orphaned elephants being fed at this transit park prior to hopefully being released into local National Parks. A simple seating arrangement on concrete steps gave us a great view. Best to sit on right hand side when entering the seating/standing area.
title: Elephants a plenty.

body: We had a very pleasant trip trough the park with Lahiru. The park is huge, we could see many animals, a lot of elefants, birds, reptiles etc. He arranged transportation form/to Tangalle for us, small breakfast and water. Everything top, can recommend for sure.
title: Very nice

body: This is a place where orphaned elephants are looked after until they can be taken back to the national parks. They are orphaned due to natural reasons but also because of "man".There are currently about 50 orphans here varying in size and age. They are brought from the waters edge in 2's or 3's and know exactly where their milk is, which is dispensed though a tube. Once they have drunk they move onto something that is in a trough. This public feeding is done twice a day and the entrance fee goes towards the upkeep on the home. There is also an interesting little museum explaining about the cycle of elephants and the difference between Sri Lankan and African elephantsThe reason I didn't give this 5* was that I saw the staff using sticks on the elephants to get them into the correct position for the milk and then to "encourage" them to move on
title: Such dedication to these orphaned elephants

body: The baby elephants are so beautiful that they drink milk. This is left open 3 times a day. We went twice. Such a wonderful experience. Elephant activities were a new experience for us. We have never seen it this way. If you come to Udawalawe it is a must go place.
title: Baby Elephant paradise

body: Seeing a baby elephant suckling is a beautiful experience. The way they run to the milk jug in order is so adorable.
title: Baby elephant paradise

body: Easy to find just a few miles along the road from Uduwalawe National Park. The main thing to see here is feeding time, which I believe is every three hours from 9am. The ticket office opens about 15 minutes before feeding, so you can comfortably walk to the viewing platform before the elephants arrive (I recommend standing at the right-hand end of the platform as you face the paddock for the best photo opportunities). At feeding time, the rescue elephants are released into the paddock, a few at a time, where they are fed a mix of nutrients in milk and water that they really enjoy. Then they're shepherded towards the guests at the viewing platform where there's a big pile of leafy tree branches for them to eat. These are all rescue elephants being brought back to full health before being released back into the national park, so it's for a good cause too.
title: Elephant Sanctuary

body: Came to the transit home after a jeep safari in the National Park.Over 50 elephants counted, including many babies. We were there at feeding time which was quite amusing as the elephants were jostling for the food! Interesting to see but not entirely sure where the elephants go after being here?
title: Good experience watching the elephants

body: I visited this site because I wanted to be sure that the elephants were well looked after. It apparently was linked to the BornFree project however I wasn’t too convinced. To be fair I saw only kindness towards the elephants who journey into the compound a couple of times a day to be fed with foliage and milk. From my somewhat truncated (!) visit I learned very little about where they came from and where in fact they were likely to be transferred to. I guess it’s better than a lot, no elephants in chains but being a voyeur gave it a rather zoo like approach.I love elephants I love to see them but maybe better to leave them in the “wild” and watch them on the TV!Thankful that there was no rides/washing etc but always feel that it could move this way.I would be much happier paying a lot more to probably go to a hide in the jungle to watch them but that’s my view.I wouldn’t return.
title: Better than some I guess!

body: babies are hit with sticks even on there delicate trunks. Very upsetting, they all seemed frightened. Where are their mothers, so many babies? Tourist attraction at expense of the baby elephants. This is my second review of the place as my first was deleted....which says it all don't you think.
title: terrible don't go.

body: This to my mind was like a circus, bringing the babies in to be bottle fed so many at a time and some who were slow got moved on so quickly by who I would say was a mahout wielding a large cane. I did not like what I saw. So different from the Sheldrick centre in Kenya you never a see a stick or cane this upset me somewhat.
title: Gorgeous babies but........

body: It was so lovely to see the elephants especially the baby ones. They only let so many into the compound at one time and to see them literally running towards the milk makes you smile or laugh out loud. A wonderful sight to watch and so worthwhile.
title: Fantastic

body: This was an interesting visit to see feeding time for the "baby " elephants. There is a range of ages and sizes but the antics of some just make you laugh. Sad that there are so many orphans but the need is there and this Transit Home achieves the end goal. Please visit dont be put off.
title: Good experience

body: The elephant transit home is one of the most amazing places I have ever visited. The orphaned elephants are so well cared for and feeding time is a wonderful site. No gimmicks, no getting too close, just observing in their natural environment, preparing them to live life to the full as a wild elephant should. I cannot think of a better way of spending a few hours.
title: Elephant transit home

body: the local call it elephant orphanage, you get to see how injured elephant and baby ones are treated before they release them to the wild...i think they feed the elephants three times a day so please check the time before you get there, the place is well maintained any you sit under a shelter to watch the elephant eat and have a bath in the water
title: good place for good reason

body: To watch the Elephants being fed & watching them interact has been excellent and informative. Close enough to see the animals without disturbing them too much. A must do experience if you are in Sri Lanka.
title: A great experience

body: Loved watching the elephants get fed and the small information centre had some really interesting displays to learn lots about the Asian elephants and the threat to their environment. Definitely worth a visit
title: Very enjoyable and informative

body: A couple of times a day you can have a look how the baby elephants getting their food. They start to run towards the place where they’ve their milk and this is very cute. Very nice to see how the animals are getting the care they needed. There is also an information center about the elephants. We had an hour stay and it was good fun.
title: Very cute

body: A very worthwhile visit. Suggest getting seated 20 mins early if you’re on the 1200 booking to sit at the front.
title: Great experience

body: This park is doing wonderful work to protect baby elephants that have been abandoned or injured in the wild. We attended one of the feedings and it was incredible to watch the baby elephants drink milk through a hose and funnel. Don’t miss this experience.
title: Great Experience!

body: Great value for moneyOnly 500/- entrance. Good opportunity to see elephants closely that are reintroduced back to wild. Has 4 feeding times per day.
title: Very good

body: The Udawalawe Elephant Transfer Home is a facility within Udawalawe National Park in Sri Lanka that was established in 1995 by the Sri Lanka Department of Wildlife Conservation. Its primary objective is to rehabilitate orphaned elephant calves for ultimate release back into the wild.Sri Lankan elephants (Elephas maximus maximus) are an endangered species and their survival in their natural habitats is threatened due to human activities. Elephants in the wild are constantly being killed, and many elephant calves become orphaned. In order to support these orphaned elephants, the Department of Wildlife Conservation set up the Elephant Transit Home within Udawalawe National Park with help from the Born Free Foundation.The facility was established under the 29th Amendment to the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance Part II.As of 8 February 2009, 39 orphaned elephant calves were being looked after.The elephant calves are released to the jungle after they become strong enough to survive in their natural habitats. As of 2008, sixty-five elephants had been released to the jungle. BEST PLACE FOR KIDS.
title: Best Place to see Baby Elephants

body: I was a bit suspicious about this part of our tour, but in the end I realised what the transit home are trying to achieve.. Its a great place to see how orphaned elephants are cared for until they are 5 years old and can be released into the park .... You are seated near enough to see the little elephants, being fed, but far enough away not to be a distraction...
title: Good to see....

body: I was there today and I was very shocked by the way the animals were handled. A rope was tied around the foot of a small elephant, then it was locked away by 4 men. nobody explained why that happened.
title: Shoked

body: I thought you would be closer to the action than this and hadn't realised that getting involved in feeding the baby elephants was on very limited occasions only - it happens for a special event pre-booking so few days to see it. It is very busy so you all sit in a stand a bit away and watch the elephants arrive, rather than you being taken to them. I know this is better for the elephants so they don't get spooked by the humans and can be left in their own habitat but just to make people aware this is how it is done. It's down to luck as to how far the elephants come towards you, most stayed fairly well back when I was there. I saw elephants much closer when on our coach and on 2 separate occasions they were strolling out in the wild past our bus window. Better experience at Yala too. If you have never seen elephants and want to be able to observe them then book this up. Otherwise....
title: Good but not what I was expecting

body: Read some reviews on here saying that the calves were hit with sticks but we didn’t see any being beaten. A couple of staff did have sticks but just used them to guide the calves over to the herd.We arrived for the 9am feed and it wasn’t busy. You can’t get near to the calves but watch them from a viewing area. It was truly wonderful watching the calves of varying ages take their milk from bottles and suckling tubes. Once old enough they will be returned to the park to integrate with other elephants. Visited the information centre afterwards which was very informative and there is the skeleton of an elephant also which made interesting reading. Stalls where you can buy trinkets or drinks are also just outside.
title: Loved it.

body: this a best place to see the tiny elephant babies.During the feeding time (9.00/12.00/3.00) we can see the unforgettable activity of the baby elephant
title: baby elephant feeding

body: I was really surprised to discover this place, I am always really suspicious when it is about a place where animals are treated by humans, but I was a very good experience, this transit home is very peaceful for teh elephants an dthey are treated well. (from what I could see). I recommand to come when it is feeding time.
title: PEACEFUL PLACE FOR ELEPHANTS

body: I’m usually uneasy about wildlife out of the wild but this centre is helping to conserve the population by raising orphaned elephants and then releasing them back to the wild once they’re 5. They are also tracking them as adults to gain more knowledge and focus conservation efforts. It was wonderful to observe the elephants enjoying their food and milk. We also liked the information centre which gave interesting details in English, Sinhalese and Tamil.
title: Conservation not entertainment- as it should be.

body: We visited this site as part of a G Adventures tour of Sri Lanka. We watched the 12 noon feeding of the baby Elephants. What fun! They certainly did not leave any of the branches that had chopped down for them. The museum of elephants attached to this facility was also excellent and I learned some new facts about elephants.
title: Baby Elephants Feeding

body: This collection of largely smaller elephants put on a good show. There probably was fifty some elephants who got their milk during the 0900 to 0930 feeding. They were kept in a staging area before being released toward the feeding area when, knowing what was coming, many trotted forward. Most were fed by way of a hose after opening their mouths. Some of the smaller ones were individually fed from what might aptly be described as the world’s largest plastic milk bottles. After the elephants were fed, they were shunted over to an area to eat where fresh grass had been put down, a waterhole beside it. There was a cheer when a smaller elephant was finally able to have his turn feeding, never able to make his way to the feeding area. The only negative was the incessant yapping by some Brits in my group, perhaps the former colonial masters of the country thinking the sign ‘Jungle is silent, you too be silent’ did not apply to them. The experience is of course not life in the wild but relative silence is the best way to appreciate wildlife in any setting.
title: MAN AT HIS BEST

body: It's great to help contributing for the feeding of orphan elephants, despite the national parks, there are still a number of elephants killed every year on Sri Lanka.
title: Great work to save the elephants

body: The transit home is worth a visit from anyone. A large group of elephants of all ages and some good photo shots.Top Tip: Get there early to get a decent seat and bring your telephoto lens along
title: Better than expected

body: Fantastic to see all the small elephants being fed. Your definitely get some good photos here. It's amazing to see the little elephants eating the leaves and stripping the bark off the branches.
title: A must place to visit in Udawalawe

body: We arrived at about 8.30am ready for feeding at 9am. Everyone has to stand on a terrace behind a ditch separating you from the elephants. There were well over 100 people there.Best place to stand/sit is on the right hand side.The elephants gather in an adjacent field and patiently wait by the gate and then they are let into the feeding paddock 3 or 4 at a time.They run (trumpeting) to the feeding station where the are fed milk through a funnel and tube and then they eat palm leaves left out for them. Some of the younger elephants don't yet have full control of their trunks, so they are hand fed, but it's interesting watching these young elephant trying to feed themselves.On the face of it, it's a bit "feeding time at the zoo", but this facility looks after so many baby elephants up to the age of 5 and has released well over 100 back into the wild. The elephants do live as if in the wild, the orphanage provide food and medical care. The information centre is well worth a visit and you do have the opportunity to make a donation
title: Baby Elephants! What's not to love!!

body: The tremendous work being done to raise up young orphaned elephants is demonstrated when you visit the centre. You can watch the feeding of these beautiful animals; some very young ( oh so cute!) and some starting to grow and throw their weight around. The feeding times are 9,12,3 and 6 and it is best to arrive about thirty minutes early. You will be thrilled to see how the milk is fed to the elephants as they are being weaned to start eating real food; leaves and branches. Well worth the 500 rupee entrance fee per person. Small information centre is worth a look too as it explains what is happening with the transit program. A must do in Udawalawe!
title: A must see in Udawalawe!

body: Orphaned elephants from all over Sri Lanka are cared for at this facility with 116 having been released into the wild & about 16 new babies born in the wild from these elephants (with only about 3000 in the wild this is a significant number). Our ticket money goes towards the raising of these babies. Its not a smick/flash operation but you can see the baby elephants being fed (sooo cute). There is also a grown elephant with prosthetic leg (he wont be released) that they care for - just amazing to see him get about. There are several sessions to watch the feeding, sit on the right side of stand for the best view.
title: Thank goodness this facilty exists

body: This amazing facility rehabilitates orphaned baby elephants from birth to 5 years of age. The elephants live in the wild but four times a day they turn up at the gates to be fed milk etc. It was incredible to watch the babies some only a few months old run to the feeding troughs where they are hand fed. Its a fantastic opportunity to witness the different personalities of elephants - quiet, hold back, reserved while others are pushy, rude, and extroverted. One of my family's favourite experiences in SL.After the feeding don't miss walking through the Information Centre and learn some very interesting facts on these beautiful creatures.
title: A Sri Lankan Must Do

body: Elephant transit home in Udawalawe is a must see attraction if you are visiting the park/ passing byThere's 3 feeding times at 9.00am, 12.00noon, 3.00pm and 6.00pm and the ticket counters open 15 mins prior to each sessionWe went at the 3.00pm and was fascinated to see almost 100 elephants coming in for the feeding sessionThe facilities are not top class so don't expect any kind of luxuries. The overall experience will last about 30 mins.
title: A must See Experience

body: A must visit. These people are doing amazing work rescuing, raising and releasing orphaned baby elephants. Watching the baby elephants be fed be bottle feed will make your heat melt. Suitable for all ages. Make sure you know the feeding times and be there and be ready in time. For us is was a long detour back to get to the facility which could have been avoided if we had planned this inclusion into the itinerary......but we were very glad we made the detour.
title: Wow wow wow

body: This orphanage was established in 1995 and is part of the department of wildlife conservation. On average they feed around 40 elephants five times a day as long as they need to before getting released in the park itself. The 55 workers of the ETH doing a fantastic job, they really care about the animals and treat them absolutely correct! No elephant is getting hurt while feeding, they just use thin wooden sticks to guide them, to make sure every elephant gets something to eat. If you want to support an ethical operating organisation, then choose this one over Pinawala or others. I have been in close contact to the main vet over the last nine years and I can absolutely guarantee you that they're doing their best. I was at the lunch feeding again today and saw so many little baby elephant orphans which come from all over Sri Lanka to the ETH. So cute, you will love it. Do a safari through the actual national park afterwards to see the big ones roaming free in the wild.
title: Very good experience

body: It is interesting to see how feed small elephants!Will be very interesting for small kids, but not only !
title: Visit

body: This is an organisation which looks after orphaned elephants. They hand feed them 3 times a day. Entrance is a minimal fee. You can also sponsor them in several ways. Well worth a visit.
title: Awwww!!

body: We visited this site some days ago before we do the safari. It is a small place with an area that has many information and interesting things regarding life, history and behaviour of these amazing animals. After this is another area where you can sit around 20 meters far from the elephants and look the baby elephants getting fed and how they behave and react. It is funny and interesting because their behaviour is very close to our behaviours. The thing that amazed me a lot was how good an elephant with immobility problems is trated and cared by the staff.The area is not so well organised and looks like dirty which this should be change.
title: Cute Baby Elephants

body: Great 1/2 day trip. Interesting guide with a keen spotting eye. Lots of elephants. Highly recommended.
title: Excellent.

body: Never nice seeing baby elephants being whacked with a stick. Horses for courses, I guess, but certainly not my cup of tea.
title: Wouldn’t recommend

body: I have not been to other elephant 'centres' but I know people visit areas where the elephants are tied up with chains and controlled a lot more as they are wild animals, and to have them as such a tourist attraction, requires some control. However here, you are a distance away from the elephants and there are soooo many. Unlike a safari, you are guaranteed to see a tonne of elephants (or a fair few tonnes...!!) getting fed their milk and eating leaves. As some other reviews mention, there is a man with a stick. However, I think to ensure the feeding all runs smoothly, the stick is lightly used to move on the elephants and to stop the cheeky elephants shouting out for more milk or even sneakily turning around and trying to join the queue again (absolutely hilarious to watch). Go at the times they feed as you aren't allowed in much earlier and you won't spend more than 45mins there but it is definitely worth it.
title: Good place to visit to support elephant welfare

body: This was a lovely visit and we saw far more elephants than we expected. We visited at feeding time and saw approximately 40 elephants, mostly babies, being fed milk and then feeding themselves on leaves. The elephants appeared well cared for and the aim is to get them back into the wild. Visitors are not allowed to interact with the elephants but watching them was very nice to see them so close up without being disturbed. We would recommend a visit.
title: Elephant conservation

body: Four of us visiting Uda Walawe National Park visited the Elephant Transit Home in the morning on 27th November 2019. The facility is situated adjacent to the Uda Walawe reservoir at the western end of the National Park. The billboard outside the facility indicated the feeding times to be at 0900, 1200 noon, 1500 and 1800 – every day. The tickets cost Rs 500 for adults and Rs 250 for children below 12 years. The cost of entry tickets to locals is Rs 20. We obtained our tickets and proceeded to the Viewing Platform and seated ourselves on the steps to see the feeding spectacle at 0900. There is no contact between elephants and visitors. Any human contact, even with the staff is minimal to prevent the elephant getting familiar with human beings as the ultimate objective is to release them back to the wild. All elephants here are orphans, mostly babies and little ones. The objective is to release them back to the wild when they can take care of themselvesAt 0900, the first elephant calves came into the feeding area – crying for milk and racing towards the feeding area. The elephant babies were fed milk using a large funnel with a long tube they could suck on. They were released into the feeding area in twos or threes so that the feeding staff could handle the commotion. It was interesting to see them turning back for seconds. Altogether there were about 40 elephants, calves and young ones. After their milk, they proceeded to the open area where there were sugar cane leaves to feed on. It was a lively spectacle while it lasted.The elephants are looked after at the feeding centre until they are five years old. While here, they are free to roam in a large area within the National Park. Once they are old enough and ready to take care of themselves, they are released back into the wild in a group.“Namal”is a juvenile elephant with a fitted prosthetic limb. It appeared that the rule about “no human contact” did not apply to him presumably because he would never be released to the wild. We saw him being physio-therapied by a specialist.I was very impressed by the true conservation effort and work done here unlike at other locations where they are trained for the enjoyment of humans!!
title: Elephant with a prosthetic Limb – Conservation at its best!

body: Make this a follow on to a safari tour of the Udawalawe National Park where you will see lots of elephants in their natural habitat. Feeding time is at 3.00pm so organise your trip accordingly. 500 Rupees entrance fee so well worth a visit
title: Lots of baby elephants!!

body: The transit centre is the only way I would recommend going to an orphanage in Sri Lanka. The humans are kept well away from the elephants who are brought up to the feeding station where they are not touched by the handlers just offered milk via big tubes over the wall of the feeding hut. They are then free to continue to walk over to the foliage left in front of the viewing area. There are so many baby elephants which is both lovely to see but sad that they are orphans. The centre asks all guest to keep noise to a minimum so as not to frighten the elephants and when they have finished feeding they wonder off down to the reserve again. Our guide told us that several orphanages have approached the transit centre to buy elephants so they can use them for commercial use to attract visitors which the transit centre refuses to do. I hope this is true and they continue to work with such care of these vulnerable creatures.
title: This is the right way to support orphaned elephants

body: Seemed good for the animals - we could not get close. Loads of babies - about 45. We went at 5;30 so got a bit darker to take ideal photos. Not many people when we went only about 30. Money and time well spent )was there about an hour)
title: Great

body: The Sri Lanka Department of Wildlife Conservation established the Transit Home in 1995 to rear and prepare orphaned elephant calves for transition back to the wild. Supported by the Born Free Foundation and a number of sponsors which included our tour company, Travelmarvel, it is an ethical place and a safe haven for the animals. We arrived for the 9.00am feeding time, the viewing platform already crowded; funds raised from admissions of LKR500 for adults and LKR150 for children help fund the upkeep. Much excitement as the animals came into view, an then, silence and sad murmurs as it was noticed that the lead elephant had a pronounced limp. It was Namal, wearing a leg prosthesis donated by Cologne Zoo. I doubt anyone minded that he was receiving personal attention. Afterwards, calves of varying ages were allowed entry to the feeding area in orderly manner to receive their milk rations.Although it is certainly a tourist attraction, it does remarkable work. The elephant is an endangered species, and to date, over 100 calves have been rehabilitated and released back into the wild. There were over 40 calves at feeding time. The Home welcomes sponsorship or any type of practical support.
title: Rehabilitation of Orphaned Elephant Calves

body: If you love baby elephants, this is a great place to go to watch them from a distance. I was let down by how far we were from the animals, but they explained this was for humane reasons, which I can appreciate. If you're in the area, it's definitely a great way to spend an hour. Make sure you sit toward the far right so you're close to the feeding area.
title: Cute and fun to watch, but not what I expected

body: Lovely place where the rescue injured/orphaned elephants and train them to live in the wild. Just another beautiful reason to visit Sri Lanka. The babies are adorable!
title: A wonderful place

body: This is very sweet - if you are going to do a safari trip maybe do this after that so that the elephants in the national park are the first ones you see, but watching the tiny elephants run into get their milk was joyus - we went for the 6pm sunset one and it was quite magical to see them at dusk and lit up
title: Cute Visit

body: Was told we could go here and feed the elephants, in fact it's a place to stand 20m away from the elephants and take photos. Maybe we were spoilt with the safaris we had been on previous but it wasnt the best trip we've had here.
title: Little disappointing

body: we have only this place in srilanka to visit real wild baby elephants. they get 4 times a day to drink milk. i went there more than 100 times with my guest to show this unforgetable expierience. so i like to invite to you to come and visit this place.
title: Milk Feeding

body: Lovely place and well worth a visit.They do fantastic work with these animals. The elephant with a prosthetic leg was a bit uncomfortable to watch however it seemed happy enough
title: Very cute baby elephants

body: This place isnt as popular as other similar places in Sri Lanka (like Pinnewala) but was wonderful. I myself decided to go there after i had read positive reviews on tripadvisor. This place is genuine, unlike Pinnewala, and there is quite a crowd to see the baby elephants at feeding time. Feeding slots are 9.00, 12.00, 3.00 and 6.00.Seats on the right offer a better view because thats where the elephant feeding station is. It is a beautiful sight watching cute baby elephants running to get milk and pushing each other out of the way.Highly recommended for children and adults alike.
title: Wonderful experience at a genuine elephant orphanage
