body: Our first Sri Lankan visit and a real treat, making our wedding anniversary really special.Neither of us had thought that we would see so many elephants in one place and watching the feeding was wonderful, as was seeing the elephants, from a few weeks old to five years, all together. There were over fifty elephants and as well as being fed they learn from each other. Our guide Surendra was able to explain the process from care to independence for the elephants.
title: An anniversary treat

body: ETH does very good work taking care of orphaned elephants and making sure they are kept free and with little human contact. I understand they need the visitors to help keep the place. I can also believe the idea that they need to be controlled, or the place would become chaos, and that they are so thick skinned that they don't really feel when "the man with the stick" hits them. However, this was a bittersweet visit for me, as I couldn't let go of the idea that these are babies who lost their mothers, and that maybe some more sympathy towards them wouldn't hurt... If anyone from the ETH was reading, I would suggest:- a small presentation before the start about the quantities of milk (some babies seemed to want more but couldn't. Why? Maybe it's not good for them, maybe the park doesn't have enough money...), the way they are organised, why, the whole hitting them with a stick thing, etc., etc...- Someone telling the people to shut up!! All in all it was worth seeing, but be prepared to be a little sad.
title: Mixed feelings

body: Lovely to see the orphaned elephants being fed. We arrived at 9am so not too many visitors which meant we had a great view of the elephants being brought in to get their milk. Nice to hear how the animals are cared for until their eventual release at 5years old into one of Sri Lanka’s National Parks. Well worth a visit.
title: Lovely experience

body: Very lovely to see the babies coming through to be fed. Nice to see a venomous snake on the tree roots on the way.
title: Feeding time at the zoo......

body: If you aren’t going to do a safari then this is a perfect place to see baby elephants.There is a viewing area and the elephants are let in. We went at the 6pm feeding and it was a little dark and there were a fair few moths hassling us. I would go in the day if my bus had got to Udawalawe a little earlier.
title: Great opportunity to see baby elephants

body: I am very wary of elephant places in Asia but this was a good experience. The good: no elephant rides, no contact with the visitors. The bad: there was too much noise. Loads of locals and they kept talking. Must be stressful for some of the elephants. Better than Pinnawela though.
title: Good experience

body: This was an impressive way to see young elephants up close. This centre cares for young elephants and eventually releases them into the national Park nearby. Visitors see how the calf's are milked and there was some funny moments during the feeding.
title: Great wildlife experience.

body: Their was elephants care place and peoples can meet baby Elephant to old elephants in same please . Also some injured elephants was their and care them on humans . The elephants activities can see very closly and calmly .Thanks .
title: The Elephants

body: We saw sooooooo..... many elephants, some babies and some much older.We saw 1 which had lost a leg to a land mine with a false leg...my family and I had a a wonderful time see the elephants feeding and even gave a donation so the elephants were looked after..
title: Lovey place to visit with or without children.

body: Seeing the baby and juvenile elephants being fed was excellent. A really lovely experience seeing them run, feed and some even having little tantrum
title: Fabulous

body: This is a lovely attraction and well run centre. The feeding time at transit home are at 9am, 12pm, 3pm, 6pm daily and lasts around 30-40 mins with a walk around the information centre after. It costs 500 Rupees per adult and the kids pay half. We thoroughly enjoyed watching the elephants come running for their milk. It was like a show when one of the smallest of elephants and obviously new to the routine kept trying to go back for more - They let him off a few times and did need to push him with the stick, you may flinch at that but elephants have such thick skin so would feel a tap! Having seen several elephant places, this was well run. We had seen it on a BBC program before we came.
title: Worth a visit

body: This place does an amazing job to feed all the young elephants. We went to the 3pm feeding, it was quite crowded with school children so to get the best view get there early and sit on the right hand side. There were so many baby elephants that needed help that it is a little sad, also, one keeper kept hitting and poking the elephants with a stick to move them on. Some of the greedier ones did need moving away from the feeding station but there has to be a better way than by hitting them. It is still a valuable charity that helps orphaned elephants and the 500 rupees to get in is reasonable.
title: Mixed feelings

body: Adorable elephants. So gorgeous. One guy kept hitting them with a stick though which was horrible to watch. Overall I think the charity do really good work though and really help the plight of these orphaned elephants. Only 500r to get in. Get there 20 mins early and sit to the right if you want a good viewing area.
title: Good place to support charity

body: We visited for 12 o’clock feeding time on our way to Yala. It was wonderful to see the young elephants running in for their milk, absolutely adorable! It was just so sad that there were so many needing help. There was a sign up saying that they accept donations of milk or money, but we didn’t see anybody we could ask about this and as we were in a rush, left feeling rather guilty as we had wanted to donate to them. I think this needs to be made easier with donation boxes or something, especially as they only charge such a small entrance fee. This is a wonderful place, please do visit if you are in the area!
title: Fantastic Place.

body: So having seen the reviews I booked the 12pm feed. All appeared fine until one of the feeders starting hitting one of the smaller elephants to move away from the feeding area. I was looking in another direction and the noise made me turn towards the feeding platform to witness the hitting. Whilst I appreciate they need to move them on to allow for more elephants to be fed the amount of hits was uncalled for!!!!! I would not visit again!!
title: Poor Treatment

body: Loved our visit here watching the elephants being fed and then bathing in a pool afterwards. It is obvious the staff love their jobs looking after the elephants, the babies were adorable. It was refreshing that no souvenirs were on sale and it didn’t feel touristy. If you are in the area we totally recommend you visit the transit home.
title: Loved our visit

body: This was not a part of our itinerary. Thankfully Danesh from Mowgli Safari recommended this to us. Feeding time at Orphanage happens at 9am, 12pm, 3pm, 6pm daily. The whole event lasts 30-40 mins. Adults are 500 Rupees each, kids get a discount. It’s well worth a visit. Watching all the elephants run in for their milk, especially the babies was so much fun. We really enjoyed it!
title: Watch the baby elephants feed

body: It was really nice to see the work that goes into looking after orphaned and injured elephants. The little baby elephants were very cute when they got all excited about feeding time. The only thing that I think would be beneficial is a donation box. I donated some extra money at the end but I had to do this at the ticket entrance. I think more people would donate for this great cause if it were more obvious on where to donate.
title: Great work done to help elephants

body: The ETH is an ethical non-profit orphanage for baby elephants who they care for and raise before releasing to the wild at the age of 5-6. You can watch the elephants being fed at 9, 12 or 3 but you cannot touch them. This is because they need to minimise human contact to give the babies the best chance of thriving in the wild as normal elephants. Stay away from places that encourage touching or feeding the elephants, with the exception of the Elephant Freedom Project which is not an orphanage but an elephant rescue and is still a good place to support. The ETH elephants are never chained and roam free in beautiful big open fields. A very special experience which we are glad we had.
title: The only elephant orphanage to visit

body: We had the wonderful (if short) visit to the Elephant Transit home. We were informed the baby feeding times were at 9, 12, 3 and 6. We arrived at 11.15 assuming there would be opportunity to look around and gather information about the home before the feeding. However the gates did not open until 11.30. At this time there was a large crowd so we chose to buy our tickets and go straight to the viewing area. (Tickets for adults were 500rps and children up to 12 were 250rps- we did not have to pay for our 2 and 6 year old!)We had been advised to find seating to the right as this gives a clearer view of the elephants entering and feeding. (Good advice).Whilst waiting there was a young elephant roaming around the with a metal collar around its neck. We were not sure or informed what this was for but hoped it was in preparation for its release and a tracking mechanism.At 12 the feeding began and it was spectacular to observe. It lasted about 30 minutes and after being fed it was great observing the young elephants grazing and wallowing in the water.We were however disappointed to observe one mahoot/ staff member on his phone the entire time and use a wooden stick on the elephants legs.Before leaving we had opportunity to look around the information centre which my 6 year old thoroughly enjoyed as he gathered useful facts, looked at skeletons and looking at art work.Would recommend as a short trip as there work is invaluable.
title: Soooooo many baby elephants

body: A lovely experience despite hot and dusty conditions- we went on full moon day so extremely busy with locals too but everyone had a good view of the elephants feeding- they are so funny to watch
title: Cute elephants

body: Watching the babies come for the feedings was an incredible experience that should not be skipped. The Elephant Transit Home does great work caring for the orphans while preparing them for life in the wild. The home also cares for an adult elephant who is missing a foot and has a prosthetic foot to wear during the day. The tufts of hair on the babies' heads were just adorable. Also, plan time to visit the Elephant Transit Home shop. There isn't a huge selection, but there are beautiful wooden carvings and elephant statues and all the proceeds go to caring for the elephants under the center's care.
title: Absolutely Adorable!

body: This was lovely, seeing the baby elephants rushing over to be bottle fed, and the older ones fed by tube and funnel, before snacking on grasses. While spectators are kept apart, on raised seating, you are close to the elephants and can see clearly. Great photo opportunities! Well worth the visit - and your entry fee helps fund the work.
title: Not to be missed!

body: One of the most beautiful places I have been in my life.All that baby elephants... treated with care and love.You must visit and help because here they do a wonderful job.No rides! no exploitation! You go SEE the animals.Wonderful!
title: Wonderful work.

body: Everyone should come and watch the baby elephants being fed. Humane treatment where the elephants wander in for milk and banana leavesEnjoyed every minute watching them all have their milk
title: Feeding elephants

body: We visited here in April the day before our Safari and it was a lovely hour or so to watch the young having milk, we only just scraped in in time for the 3pm session, sadly afterwards, nothing else seemed to be open - we did buy some milk for the elephants though as every little bit helps as it is a charity.
title: Enjoyable Visit

body: If you are already in the Udawalawe area, you have to go here. Its a half an hour feeding, so would only take an hour out of your day; yet it is completely worth it to see the different elephants of all ages, coming in for feeding
title: If you’re in the area, go!

body: Was amazed at the number of elephants all eager to have a drink of milk! Baby Ellie’s adorable as always. Was hoping for info on possibly adopting an elephant to help support their work but this information wasn’t available but found out via the Born Free Foundation after my visit.
title: Lovely experience

body: I suppose it might be fair to say that ETH is like the Kenya's Sheldrick Elephant Orphanage of Sri Lanka? From what we could see? There were over 45 little elephants that paraded out when we went to watch their 6pm feeding, and they were quite adorable (and surprisingly loud!). One thing that made it different from Sheldrick, though, was a lack of audience interaction and education. I would have liked to have been able to learn more about the elephants' plight in Sri Lanka and what we can do to help. On their website it shows that you can foster an elephant for 25,000 rupees per month, which is much higher than the $50 per year at Sheldrick. I wish there were other clear ways provided by ETh to attract tourist's generosity and educate...
title: Adorable elephants, but more education opportunities needed

body: We enjoyed seeing all the elephants at the Elephant Transit Home & also happy to give a donation to help with the great work try do here. The many baby elephants are hugely popular of course. Recommend seeing this one
title: ETH - many elephants

body: I was skeptical having been to similar places that were AWFUL. This is not. Seems to be offering elephants a safe home and rehabilitation and special residents such as the bull elephant maimed in a land mine... the babies are heart breakingly cute and seem to be in safe hands. Good interp centre too. Worth a visit and some $$
title: Surprisingly worth it

body: Feeding time at ETH happens at 9am, 12pm, 3pm, 6pm daily. The whole event lasts 30-40 mins. Adults are 500 Rupees each, kids get a discount. It’s well worth a visit. Watching all the elephants run in for their milk, especially the babies was so much fun. We really enjoyed it. You could see that the elephants were well looked after by the people who run the place. The only shame was that the Information Centre and Shop were both closed after the feeding session. There was also no guide available for questions. Consequently there was little or no information for visitors. There was a sign about donating to the centre but nothing else. I think people would happily support the ETH but they need to provide bodies on the ground to get their message out to people.
title: Great fun for the whole family

body: We went for the 9am feed, it was rammed with school kids and local families but it was definitely a highlight. I never knew how fluffy baby elephants were!! Loved the bellowing for extra milk! This gets four stars as it would have been better if they had told us a bit more about the work they were doing there.
title: Very busy but worth it!

body: We visited here before our safari took place and were glad to see it is just as good as the Sheldrick foundation. All the elephants here are orphaned and are set to be released into the wild when they are able to be. The public are allowed to see the feeding time from a viewing platform that gives a really good place to take photos. They are not there long but it’s still worth the trip. The smallest seemed the loudest and most boisterous. There is a small museum and gift shop and you can register donations as you leave by approaching the staff in booths. I think they could advertise where to donate clearer as I think they miss out on lots of opportunity to maximise the support where people may be unaware of how to donate
title: Great experience

body: Highly recommend a visit here - the baby elephants are utterly adorable as they run in together to be fed. It is mesmerising watching them - we sat for a long time watching them interacting together. Ticket price goes to support the work of rehabilitating orphaned elephants - we subsequently saw an Elephant in Udawalawe National Park with a tracker collar on him, and our guide said he was one of the elephants saved by the transit home and released back into the wild.
title: Baby Elephants!!!!!!!

body: Nice visit despite the huge crowds. We landed for feeding time at 12 and all gathered in a stand to watch the elephants come (bit artificial if you do a safari the same day) nonetheless the little elephants all come running through to get their milk and you will get some giggles at their personalities and antics. It lasts about 30 mins and then we visited the information centre attached. The centre is fairly basic but the info good. It’s a worthy cause and entrance fee is 500RP each (€2.50)
title: Feeding time

body: Pity to see so many orphaned or disabled elephants but it was enjoyable watching them feeding. Big crowd in the stands but we found a spot on the far right which had a good view.
title: enjoyable

body: We went yesterday and enjoyed every minute.All of the emphasis is put on the well being of the elephants and we saw no examples of mistreatment whatsoever.There are no shows,tricks,or presentations it’s all about the care and health of these wonderful creatures.I hope everyone who is in the area visits here as they can clearly do with all the financial support they can get .Thank you for a wonderful experience.
title: Fantastic experience

body: Seeing the elephants was my main inspiration in visiting Sri Lanka.This (under-funded) orphanage is well worth a visit. Visitors view the elephants at feeding times from a platform; there is no interaction with the tourists or displays, such as playing games or other enforced activities to entertain the public. The elephants are kept in as natural a setting as possible in order to return them to the wild when they are around 5 years old. Most of the staff seem caring - however, there was one man who seemed overly keen on prodding and hitting the little elephants with a stick. I realise that these are wild animals and there needs to be some control but he was over-aggressive in my view. I also believe that the "silence" notice should be better enforced - some of the tourists were loud and disrespectful of the elephants natural setting.
title: A highlight of my trip - marred by one man with a stick!

body: This was a great 30 minute stop between ella and the coast .It is reasonably priced ,considering what it does and was a unique experience.Lot's of young children enjoying the feeding of young elephants' happy place.
title: Great place to stop between ella and mirissa

body: I read about the elephant transit home and I was impressed with what they said they do for the elephants. However, when we got there for the 12pm feeding time there was a man who hit a few of the elephants even the baby ones forcefully with a stick. This was highly distressing to see and I felt as though it was completely unnecessary. I left immediately after this happened and I wish I never went to begin with.
title: Avoid.

body: My family and I (a group of 7) can see that, big picture, the centre is doing good by releasing elephants back into the wild. HOWEVER, we all left early because of the violence that we were seeing. Baby elephants being hit hard and threatened with big sticks (the elephants were clearly afraid) just because they wanted more milk. It brought tears to our eyes and we left. It was so distressing.We were also part of a huge, loud crowd. We and some others were quiet, but most people were so loud and disrespectful. There needs to be people enforcing quiet. The centre lets in too many tourists, clearly just to maximise money. The staff are cruel to the elephants infront of the crowd. I can’t imagine what they are like without an audience.The centre should learn from conservationists such as Lek Chailert, and run a sanctuary without violence. People like her have proven that it CAN be done. That’s why she was given an award by Hilary Clinton.
title: Hitting Elephants

body: This place is fantastic. A lovely place to see baby elephants being fed and cared for. We got there early for the 9am feed and got good seats to watch the baby elephants feeding and thoroughly enjoyed it. It was wonderful to see and brought a tear to my eye (It’s supported by the Born FreeFoundation).My only criticism was that one of the workers was hitting the elephants - not a gentle tap or even a little smack when needed, but big heavy hits with a stick and sometimes it was unnecessary. I didn’t like this. I also think this place is missing a trick and could be earning more money/donations for the elephants by doing the following;1 - Having more donation boxes scattered around the place for people to donate money2 - doing a sponsor an elephant where people can choose an elephant and sponsor for a one off fee or monthly and receive a photo and certificate once a year. If you visit this place please leave a donation. 100% donation goes to buying the baby elephants’ milk (you get a receipt) and this place gets no help from the government but the government takes a percentage of gage receipts.
title: Great place - could easily make more money

body: It was just lovely to see the baby and young elephants being fed and cared for. Although you are in a stand you are still quite close. It was quie moving watching them be fed and then playing in the mud afterwards.They information centre was nicely laid out too.Well worth a visit
title: Really fabulous to watch at feeding time

body: Wasn't sure what to expect but was pleasantly surprised. Lots of baby elephants (in itself a tragedy though knowing something terrible has happened to the mothers) being looked after by caring staff. Went to the 12 noon feeding and was so moved we went back to the 9am feeding the next day. Both feeds were different, in that the second day we went the staff took the babies more out in the open for the feed and it was much easier to see them. Also saw a snake jump in the pond in front of us and catch a frog!Only downside on the second day was an act of cruelty by a staffer who hit a very young baby very hard on the trunk with his stick. He was the only one who did this as the others all used their sticks as guides to move the babies on and not as weapons. For management there, if you want to follow up it was a fellow on 26 March 2019, 9am feeding. Totally unnecessary to be so hard on a tiny baby elephant.Take time to go into the museum as the info is excellent and well put together.Apart from the nasty fellow we witnessed, I thought it was overall a great place doing really good work. I'd like to see the elephant with the prosthesis fitted with a new one as I don't think it is fit for purpose any more. Kudos for trying to help it though.
title: Baby elephants galore

body: We visited this organisation because of their affiliation with the Born Free foundation so feel they are reputable. Feeding times are 9, 12, 3 and 6. We attended the midday feeding and went back for the 6 o’clock feeding as it was just so beautiful. I got rather emotional as the elephants came running up for their milk trumpeting when they wanted more than their allowance! It’s so sad to see so many small elephants without their Mums but amazing to hear that many go back into the wild and have their own babies. The only downside is down to the visitors... signs clearly ask visitors to watch in silence and this request is ignored!! Very frustrating to see as this is surely hindering the rehabilitation of the elephants. The information center was really interesting so worth a visit and some time to read the exhibitions. They gratefully receive donations and we bought some milk powder from a local shop and took it with us on our second visit. Made us feel good knowing we were helping in some other way.
title: Amazing place getting orphaned elephants back into the wild

body: Our group stopped here for feeding of the orphans. The majority of our tour group participated in a donation for milk powder for the orphans. There is a shop which sells guidebooks which was really good. The information centro is very good explaining the history of the site. The only thing i found distressing was when the some of the orphans trumpeted wanting more milk.
title: Great that they are helping the orphans

body: Very caring staff looking after orphaned elephants many of whom are still just babies. Lots of photo opportunities and a. Sry moving experience to see these creatures being really cared for
title: Brilliant place well worth a visit

body: We visited at 12 noon which is one of the feeding times for the baby elephants. They are fed every 3 hours. Naturally the site was packed with tourists but there is a viewing area that can accommodate many people. It was a wonderful sight to see the elephants running, four at a time to the feeding station where they are fed milk through a long tube. The tiny ones are bottle fed. They then can eat grass or play in the waterhole. The whole sssion lasts about 30 minutes. There is also an information centre where you can learn more about the elephants in Sri Lanka.
title: Visit at feeding time

body: This place is a transit place for baby elephants. They have either been left behind, injuired or sick. This place takes care of them all undtil they are about 5 years old. Then they set them free in the nature. So you can only visit this pkace when the little ones ate fed with milk every 3 hours. You can not get close to them. You can donate money or sponsor your own elephant. I do think it is a fantadtic project.
title: Lots of babyelephants

body: Lovely to see around 50 baby elephants being looked after before being released back in to the wild. Very amusing watching them sneak back for more milk and race to the milking station when the gates open. Well worth a 30 minute visit whilst in the area.
title: Baby elephants!

body: The elephants came in in small groups to feed, some by bottle, good to see close up. Only 52 young there, kept until about the age of five before being released into Uda Walawe. A good museum with interesting information about the life of an elephant. Recommend a visit.
title: Feeding time

body: Interesting place to visit, however not possible to come close to the elephants neither feed them. It is better to hire a jeep and go directly to the Udawalawe park safari where you can see elephants more close in wild nature surroundings.
title: Attraction before safari

body: We enjoyed a superb visit here. Part of a group tour, but I believe entry price is 500LKR (about £2). We went for the noon feed and witnessed 40 to 50 young orphan elephants milk fed by hand. Youngest was just a few weeks old. What a wonderful experience. Don’t miss it!
title: Excellent Conservation Project

body: Plenty of elephants, of various ages, and very entertaining watching their antics at feeding time. A good photo opportunity to see them close up and experience how well they are cared for.
title: Very enjoyable.

body: We stopped by here as part of our trip to Uda Walawe, and it was great. So many baby elephants, juvenile elephants and more. The philosophy of the organization is to save young elephants abandoned or left orphaned, but to ultimately release them back to their environment. As a result, they feed them, but not to satisfaction so that they have to continue to forage for their food naturally. It's fun to watch them feed the young elephants, and believe me the elephants are not happy when they are cut off from the powdered milk. They get angry! But they eventually walk over to the greenery on the ground and start eating that. One permanent resident is an elephant who lost part of a leg during the Sri Lanka war. They have made a prosthesis for him/her. This is a wonderful spot. Go early, because you will have to line up to get a seat.
title: Elephants galore

body: My wife and I are massive elephant fans. having travelled through much of Asia, we have been fortunate enough to ride and actually train as a mahout briefly. Therefore we probably have a more open view on the subject of elephants as tourist attractions. Here they are brought in as animals that are young and vulnerable in the wild. They are then fed and maintain their safety until they are ready to be released back to the wild. There is minimum human contact so you will only get to see them being fed from a viewing platform but in the light of recent complaints from certain 'activists' this is the true definition of animal conservation. you tube has lots if you want a peek before you go. If you are in Udawalawe for the safari, well worth the couple of quid entrance fee to help the elephants. Opens at 9 and feeding is every 3 hours.
title: how conservation should be

body: Seeing 30 baby elephants come in to feed was a highlight of our trip. They are fun to watch and cute as can be. The orphanage seems to take good care of the animals. They come in to feed in groups of 3's. You can sit on a platform to watch or stand. Feeding times are 9am, noon, 3pm and 6pm. Get there early , particularly on weekends as this is quite popular with the locals too.
title: So much fun!

body: Last week, we took a safari with Lahiru. He gets 5 stars for the safari itself and 1 star for the way he handled things start to finish. We booked a month in advance for a full day safari, which to us, meant early in the morning through park close, although we did not specify exact times, but based on the price, it was consistent with that from other info we read online. Two weeks out, we confirmed. Two days before we reached out via WhatsApp and were told we could start at 2pm because of expected bad weather, which looked perfectly clear. He said we would still get in 5 hours. Asked for a price in line with a half day and he immediately agreed which told us that he had likely double booked, nothing to do with the weather. Day of, he asks if we would be okay sharing with another person. I said our price was for private and we would like a discount for sharing. He says we’ll stay private. He shows up, asks again if we’ll share. We reluctantly agree and with no apparent communication with anyone, he picks up a woman waiting, so he clearly wasn’t waiting on our agreement. When our hotel asked when we’d be back, he said we’d be gone 3 hours. We protested that he’d said five hours and ‘oh, the park closes at 6pm’ so five hours wasn’t even possible. Ultimately we saw lots of animals, he was good at spotting them and we were away from other vehicles for the most part. So from that perspective, we were quite happy. That said, he was messaging on his phone the whole time, likely at least some with other guides, but we suspect his business has picked up more than he’s able to manage and quality has gone down. If you ask questions about the park and animals, he knows his stuff, but not in the least proactive in explaining. He was very pleased with himself every time he spotted an animal and let you know that ‘I showed you that’. It became a bit old. Overall, if you set up a safari with expectations in line, you will likely have a good experience.
title: Lahiru – good animal spotting, poor customer service

body: The guys here do an amazing job in caring for orphaned elephants. It’s a shame that it’s the interface between humans and elephants that causes youngsters to lose their parents. However it was a heart warming experience.
title: Amazing place.

body: You need to arrive early to get ticket and a good seat especially at a weekend best seats seem to be on the right hand side of the viewing platform. This is on effect a tiered concrete seating area. The orphans are adorable and charge in for their milk and then browse on cut branches. HOWEVER you can get even better view being allowed just behind the feeding station if you give a donation ahead of time they accept money of course but also milk powder. Well worth a visit also look for the owl in the trees just inside the entrance.
title: Brilliant

body: We visited the transit home for one of the afternoon feeding sessions. Fantastic. I had not expected so many elephants, I counted to 43 and then lost count. Could have sat all day and watched them feeding. Entrance costs 500 rupees, nothing really when you think how much milk they must go through! Centre opens 4 times a day, 9am, 12pm, 3pm and 6pm for feeding times and you get around 2 hours to watch, visit the shop and museum. Well worth a visit for some amazing photos and a magical experience.
title: Elephant orphanage

body: Visited as part of a group tour after the jeep safari and the perfect way to end the day. The elephants were so cute feeding and jostling around . Many locals here as well as western tourists. Worth the visit.
title: Tip: try for a seat to the right by the feeding station

body: Feeding takes place at 9, 12 and 3 daily but you should arrive around 20-30 minutes early to secure a good seat. Watching the baby elephants run through in pairs to feed was lovely and seeing the elephant with a prosthetic leg was certainly unexpected! Worth a visit if you are going to Udawalawe.
title: Lovely experience

body: Our visit happened to fall on a Bank Holiday which was very busy. We went for the 9am feed. It was amazing to see all the baby elephants queing up ready to be fed. Only 2-3 elephants are released from the queue at a time to make their way to the milk feeding station then over to grass laid out for them to eat. We watched as the older elephants encouraged the very tiny ones over to the feed. The elephants range from only months old until 5 years old before being released back into the wild. So sad to see so many elephants but lovely to see them well cared for. Make sure you visit the museum, very interesting and informative.
title: Heart warming visit

body: What a real treat Stopped off to see this home for orphaned elephants and how they show up at feeding time. First they feed them milk with a hose and then they go and graze on leaves they throw out on the ground. This is really a special opportunity and a must do.
title: Vacation

body: Visiting the Elephant left a special part of Sri Lanka with our Intrepid group. We did the 9am feed. To see these baby elephants orphans from 3months to 5 years still wild come in for their 3 hourly feed of milk and vegetation.Hints: good camera, take videos, good spot for viewing, go early, sunscreen, suitable clothing
title: Amazing Orphan Elephants

body: Who doesn't love baby elephants. So much fun watching them being fed and then playing afterwards. It can be crowded, but with patience you will end up at the front of the platform. You can take pictures.
title: So Cute!

body: We visited the transit camp after a visit to Udawalawe. It was lovely seeing the cute baby elephants coming up the field for their milk. They let in a few at a time so that they all got a chance for a feed of milk before moving over to eat vegetation that had been picked and left on the ground for them. The viewing station gives plenty of opportunity to see them up close and take photos. As previous reviewers have said you do get to see their different characters.The mahouts use their sticks to guide the elephants in the direction they should go and generally is is just a gentle tap. However, we did see one really go for it as he hit an elephant that was trying to stop a younger one getting too close to his patch of food. I did feel feel that such a brutal whack was unneccessary, although someone did say in the wild the mother would probably have given a whack with her trunk so maybe it was not as cruel as it appeared.All in all they are doing a wonderful job as these elephants are successfully released back into the wild. Definitely worth a visit and really cheap.
title: Gorgeous baby elephants

body: This place is amazing. The story behind the place can be read elsewhere but this is a lovely place to go and see baby elephants. They all seem to know the drill for feeding and a couple of naughty ones made us laugh. In answer to a previous comment about the elephants being hit with sticks we did not see any evidence of this - just a few that were gently tapped to move them on. Well worth a visit
title: Not to be missed

body: Baby elephants run for the milk and play with the other elephants was simply magical. Why are some of the elephants chained?
title: Cutest baby elephants

body: We loved this place!! It’s so nice to see the orphaned and injured elephants well cared for and looked after! We enjoyed viewing their feeding time and learning all about them after this! Highly recommend it’s a lovely thing to see and experience!
title: Wonderful place

body: We left Colombo very early and wanted to reach ETH before the feeding time. Anyway we were late and when we reached there feeding time already started. It is really interesting to watch how these baby elephants are fed. They come one by one and then the staff starts feeding them. Some times they just starts rioting with another. After they get full moved and hanging around. There were very small young elephants who became orphans due to various reasons. This is a great place and they do a very good job their by looking after these elephants. We must appreciate the fact that these elephants are released to the jungle when they grow up. I think this is a must in Sri Lanka if you are interested about the animals specially elephants.
title: Cute Baby Elephants

body: We visited Elephant Transit home whilst we were in Udawalawe to do safari. I had very mixed feelings. The good points: elephants are living free life, there were no chains, and they are returned back to wild when they are healthy and big enough. Which is really nice to know that they will live a free life. The bad points: the baby elephants seemed hungry, like there wasn’t enough milk for all of them, and when they demanded more milk they were hit with a stick, which broke my heart. They weren’t aggressive or anything and when the mahouts came close to them they started to run away anyway, so there was NO need to hit them.
title: Mixed feelings

body: For the work that is done to save these wonderful animals then it gets 5 star. Obviously feeding time is aimed at the tourists but done in a good way that the Elephants enjoy it. Keep up the good work.
title: Good work

body: Some 25 small elefants drinking milk. Ok for 30 minutes. Leave it out if you don’t have time. There were a lot of people, and don’t really got the point of it.
title: Saw it and that’s it

body: Nice to see how the staff is dealing with the elephants. It's a good thing! You should have a look. Feeding times are crowded by tourists and locals, but you will have a good view anyhow. Nice place and a fair price.
title: Cute baby elephants which are well treated

body: The Elephant Transit Home is run by the Born Free Foundation and is worth visiting to see the young orphaned elephants being fed their milk and eating the leaves. It is touristy but lovely to see the elephants being cared for and great to feel you are supporting this home.
title: Lovely to see the baby elephants being fed

body: Thought it might be a bit of a circus but how wrong can you be. A most uplifting and enchanting experience. It was moving to see how well the keepers and the elephants worked together throughout the morning feeding process from the smallest little ones to the young teenage elephants. All the personalities were there from the elephants, about 70 or so, from the naughty ones, the bolshy ones, the shy ones and the cool dudes. This is a charity not a commercial venture and will worth supporting
title: Inspiring

body: We visited the transit home and liked the animal centred focus of the conservation work here. You don’t get to interact with the elephants, but you do see them feeding at close quarters.It was amusing to watch them rush to the feeding station when it was their turn and even the youngest knew what to do. Some of the older calves tried to go back rather cheekily for a second helping, but were sent on their way by the staff. Then, they all moved on to the leafy branches right by the observation stand where we waited so there were plenty of photo opportunities. Quite rightly there was no touching since the whole focus is on eventual release for these youngsters.There’s an information centre where you can learn more about the biology and habits of the animals and the conservation work undertaken at the centre. You can make donations - all carefully recorded- with the money spent on eg milk powder for feeding the young ones.One couldn’t help but be captivated by the antics and there were certainly plenty of photo opportunities for the appreciative audience.
title: Elephant conservation

body: This is the only genuine elephant rehabilitation centre in Sri Lanka and is approved by the Born Free Foundation. As the baby elephants are returned to wild at the age of 5, no human contact is allowed so don’t expect to be allowed to feed them or ride them!!! Most of the orphaned elephants are there as a result of human - elephant conflict and there are some lovely stories on the website that show their success in reintroducing them to the wild. The baby elephants running and jostling for their milk are very cute. It is very well done with a queue for feeding and the smallest babies being fed first. We did not see anyone beating them with sticks - staff do have sticks but only used them to hit the ground to stop greedy babies trying to butt in for a second lot of milk! There are no vicious hooks or chains. The only elephant who cannot be released is a 10 year old bull with a prosthetic leg, who is clearly much loved and cared for. If you visit, please do consider giving a donation after your visit - as you leave, see the man at the gate and he gives you a receipt for your money - you state whether you wish to donate to buy milk powder or medicines.
title: Excellent project

body: Baby elephants who are too cute to handle. I'm a big fan of them. It's a home for lonely elephant babies who will be taken care until they are grown enough to fend themselves. Mostly, they will released to the Udawalawa national park when they become adults. The best is they are not caged ad free to make friends. Make sure to check the feeding times so you may get a chance to feed them if care takers allow. Kids gonna love this. Ideal for elephant lovers.
title: Baby Elephants

body: I wanted to visit this transit home after the great comments on Trip Advisor. It’s very cute how they all line up and get ready for their milk. But there was one guy there with a stick and he wasn’t afraid to use it, the elephants would run away from him as if they were scared. There was no explanation behind this myself and my partner put it down to naughty elephants and guessing the mother would do that in the wild but this was a total guess. I fully support what they are doing and releasing them back into the wild but watching him hitting the elephants with a stick was difficult.
title: Like what the home is trying to achieve. Although hitting them with a stick was hard to watch.

body: If you love animals then visiting the Elephant Transit home is a must. I also recommend that you visit during the feeding times, as it is very nice to see how pampered these beautiful elephants are
title: Beautiful herd of elephants

body: Worth a short visit before Udawalawa, it is only 5-10 minutes drive from the Ntl Parks entrance. You can have a close look at the elephant feeding, before exploring the park.
title: Worth a short visit before Udawalawa

body: Really sweet way to spend an hour watching baby elephants being fed and interacting with each other! While I waited for the feeding session I was fortunate to witness a snake hunting for frogs in the pond in front of me! Get down to the front row and avoid looking at tourists, immerse yourself in elephant pleasure’n give a donation and make yourself feel good!!!
title: If you love elephants you cannot go past!!

body: Please visit this centre rather than the orphanage where the elephants are chained up. The elephants come for food 3 times a day here. I marked it down as they whack the greedy elephants with a stick when they have had enough milk but won’t move on. Apart from that it’s a great place with good intentions for the elephants unlike the orphanage that has lost its way a bit.
title: Better than the orphanage

body: This was a brilliant morning watching the baby elephants at the feeding station. They get this 5 times a day. It was hilarious seeing how fast they run to get their share of the milk, always wanting more but having to move on. The information centre was really interesting, worth visiting. What a great job this centre does, looking after the babies until they are ready to go back to the national park. One elephant had a prosthetic leg. They survive on donations and its a fantastic facility.
title: Hilarious watching the Elephant feed

body: This place is better known as the elephant orphanage. Visits to watch feeding are at 9am, noon and 3pm. Only baby/young elephants are fed (milk) and what a sprint they can put on to reach the feeding station. One or two older, disabled elephants are also helped: one in particular has an artificial hind leg. Well worth 45 mins.
title: WELL WORTH A VISIT

body: Our guide arranged for us to visit this transit home rather than the orphanage which we had originally suggested. We are so glad that he recommended this. The elephants appear to be well cared for and no chains in sight! You do see a handler with a stick but only to move some of the more greedy youngsters away to allow others to have their turn. After their milk some of the elephants munch on greenery before they follow a cart full of sugar cane leaves away from the feeding area. The little museum is worth a visit too.
title: Well worth a visit

body: We loved this please watching the young Elephants being fed and being prepared to go back to the wild.The onsite museum is also worth a visit to understand the Elephant
title: Amazing experiance

body: I was incredibly impressed that this is a transit home and the elephants will go back into the wild. No chains like the Pinnawela Elephant Orphanage and you felt that the money you gave was doing good. This visit wasn't on our itinerary but we saw the signs and thankfully got there in time to see the feeding. Worth a visit to donate to a good cause.
title: Lotsa babies

body: We turned up just before 3pm to see the baby elephants and some bigger ones being fed.Sit on the right hand side for the best views a great 40 minutes spent being entertained by the cute elephants a must see if you are in the area.There were quite a lot of excited children having a great time seeing the elephants up close.Highly recommended
title: Elephants galore

body: Opened in 1995,ETH is doing a great job to raise the elephant calffs and send them back to the wild.
title: Awesome

body: It was wonderful to see all the baby animals getting fed. Some were very funny and had temper tantrums when the milk finished! You can not touch the elephants here, human interaction is kept to a minimum as when these elephants are grown they will be released back into the wild. It was good to see a vet on site, who was giving certain elephants eye drops. Would definitely recommend.
title: Great experience.

body: A good insight as to how the orphaned elephants are rehabilitated back into the wild. The information centre needs a good update and brighten up with perhaps some continuus video loops.
title: Informative

body: This was probably the highlight of our visit to Sri Lanka. The babies were sent in threes to get the milk, and some protested when they had to be moved away after being fed. This was the cutest scene ever, to see them running toward the feeding stand, all eager to get their milk.There was one older baby who staged a protest, even as it was being led to the feeding station, trying to walk away, trumpeting loudly! That really got all the spectators laughing.
title: The highlight of our visit!

body: We visited here before the nature reserve. U must view at the approriate feeding times and u get to see the baby elephants have their milk and stuff. U cant feed as they want to return them to free in the near by national park. It was really worth a visit. They are trying to save the orphans and injured elephants from becoming extinct and this place really helps. Toilets r ruff as. So make sure u dont want a poo. Once in the seating area we also spotted a wild snake !!!! Also if u love dogs take a snack as there a few who roam the seating area who would love somin to eat.
title: Visit baby elephants

body: This is such a lovely place to watch the handlers feed these gorgeous baby elephants. They care so much for them and it's great they get fed, then go back into the wild where they should be.They care for Namal so well too. I felt sorry for him but he seemed happy eating his sugar cane under the tree.Get there early to get a good seat to view.
title: Such an amazing experience seeing the baby elephants feed

body: We saw how the baby elephants receive milk. They were so cute. And some of then really noisy and funny
title: Sooooo cute

body: Make sure you know the feeding times and get there early to queue for entry. Sit on the right hand side and you will get the best views. It is really impressive that 10 mins before time there are no elephants and then, like they have an alarm clock, the are all there on time. Really interesting.
title: Worth a visit

body: Feeding time is 12:00 when around 40 orphaned elephants and 1 adult with a wooden leg all come around to be fed. Interesting place and no doubt does a great job in looking after these animals. Worth a visit especially if you have kids in tow.
title: Awe the wee elfulumps

body: We visited for feeding time today ahead of a safari tomorrow and found the experience amazing. We have already visited sanctuaries in Thailand where we were able to feed and bathe rescued elephants but to see so many babies being reared before being returned to the wild was something else! We arrived about 40 minutes early for the 3pm feeding and joined others who were already there. The entrance fee is low at 500 rupees per adult, once you enter there is a section to sit with a pond in between you and where the elephants will be fed. The elephants are let into the feeding area in waves, they are each fed milk by the staff and then are encouraged to head to the branches and leaves laid out for them in front of the viewing enclosure. It’s a spectacular sight once all the elephants have been let in but is bitter sweet as it shows how many have needed rescuing.Once the feeding is over there is an information centre where you can learn a lot about elephants, their history, fun facts etc.I would highly recommend this to anyone!
title: Amazing experience and informative too

body: We were pleased to find that this is indeed a true elephant refuge with interaction with humans kept to the minimum. You can watch the babies being fed from the distance and there are at least two feeding times daily. Later in Uda Walawe NP we came across a former resident wearing a tracking collar. Commercialism was very minimal, considering other such locations in the island.
title: A true refuge

body: Feeding times are at 9, 12, 3 and 6. It's a nice opurtunity to have a closer look on the orphans. This orphanage is supposed to do a rather good work with reintroducing the elephants to the wild and as far as we could judge, seem to treat them in an OK way. The baby elephants are of course adorable...
title: Close up on little elephants

body: Loved visiting here.It is not a zoo it is a transit home for orphaned elephants. They get fed every 3 hours with milk and they love it! Then they get leaves. The elephants seem really cared for even though there is a guy with a stick of persuasion, for when the elephants get greedy with the milk. The viewing area is busy, but worth the standing room or pushing locals.Would highly recommend, especially with kids! Try it, you might like it!
title: Amazing!!

body: We weren't sure that the conditions for the elephants were going to be all that they should be - our fears were totally groundless. Lovely to watch them being released in pairs and running to their milk breakfast.Well worth the visit.
title: Enchanting

body: Really nice stop off on the way to the hotel. There are fixed feeding times so check this. We went to the 6pm one which was lovely albeit a little dark toward the end.
title: Watch elephant feeding

body: This place is a must if visiting Sri Lanka. We saw 47 baby orphan elephants being fed. They are cared for until they are ready for release back into the national park. Only 500 Rupees entrance fee. To see the faces of the children visiting the centre is nearly as rewarding as seeing the elephants.
title: Wonderful place to see orphan baby elephants

body: We went to the orphanage after our safari in the Udawalawe NP. We did some research before going there, because we have read horrible things about the Pinnawala orphanage and we didn't want to support such behavior. But we found some important differences (elephants released again into the wild, not chained, less contact with humans,...) so we decided to go. After having visited it's hard to say it's a place you should put on your itinerary or should avoid:- The distance between the elephants and the public is big enough, although it would have been better if one of the guards occupied himself to keep the public quiet.- We didn't see the guards using sticks to hit the elephants, although there was one guy where the elephants seem to ran away from (they clearly knew him).- The elephants receive milk for humans, which some of them can't digest. But according to their website the exact combination of elephant milk can't yet be reproduced.- After the milk the elephants got to eat leafs and bark, although there was almost nothing left for the last group of elephants.- Some elephants seemed to be split from the group, but their website says some elephants are sick or traumatized from the human-elephant conflict and need special care for a certain period. - There is a sign at the entrance that the government of Sri Lanka is heavily supporting the orphanage.- The 'cafetaria' was donated by an animal center in Florida, USA.So we didn't see anything horrible that you can read in the worst reviews about this orphanage, but we neither can't confirm that everything is going the way it should.
title: Hard to make a judgement if you should go or avoid this place.

body: We arrived in Udawalawe in the afternoon, and we had a safari booked for the next morning so we were looking for something to do.I saw this place online so we dropped in for feeding time - it's lovely to see the baby elephants be looked after so well and to see them all drinking milk, very cute!You sit/stand in a viewing area but it is still close to the elephants so definitely worth going if in the area for something else
title: Wonderful if in the area

body: Everyone loves elephants, and visiting this place (especially around feeding time) will be most rewarding and memorable. This place performs great work by caring for orphaned elephants and returning them to the wild when possible. The elephants have unique personalities that you can see during the feeding time. We saw one forego eating to happily slosh and swim in the shallow pond while another rejected the provided plant food in favor of plucking his own gourmet grasses outside the feeding boundaries. We also saw one full grown elephant being cared for; it lost a hind leg from a land mine and its prosthetic replacement wouldn't fare well in the wild.Tourists pay more for entry than locals, but the money goes for elephant care...and profits from the gift shop go to the same noble cause.
title: Entertaining Environmentally Friendly Visit

body: Our family of 4, 2 boys aged 7 & 5, had the best time at elephant transit home. We came for the 3pm feeding. There was adequate seating and can easily observe and take photos. The elephants congregate at a gate to the far end and are released in batches of milk feeding and then they proceed to munch on leaves. Quite fascinating to watch them go through their routine. There were also some amusing interaction between the elephants and the helpers. There is also a small museum to learn more about elephants which we benefitted from. A worthy cause to help these orphaned elephants.
title: Good cause, great visit

body: A chance to see the orphaned elephants being fed. The elephants are very cute and behave just like a bunch of small children. There is a sad element to the place in that it is needed at all, 45 orphaned elephants were there when we visited however a positive is that the majority are released back to the wild.
title: High on the cute factor

body: I was a little disappointed with my visit here. Arrived to find a mass of people at the ticket office. Once we managed to get in we were directed to the viewing area which was already packed full.Watching the young elephants interacting with one another was cute but the whole experience felt far too much like a zoo/commercial enterprise than I was hoping.
title: Too crowded

body: I read comments about hitting with a stick. Thats nonsense, they have a branch inluding leafs that could never even scratch their their thick skin. It was friendly and nice to see.
title: Good

body: We were all waiting at the visitor's platform to watch the young elephants being let in from the back in small groups,many of the little ones running to get their milk at the feeding station. They then moved on to eat branches/leaves left on the ground for them. A few of the little elephants tried to sneak back to have another feed but the supervisor always noticed and the would get a telling off! Altogether it was a joy to watch and we found out that even a small elephant needs up to 14 liters of milk per day, so 60 elephants get through a lot. Well worth a visit!
title: Great Experience!

body: Feeding times are 9am, 12 and 3pm.Lovely to see the babies being fed.Viewing platform is undercover.Worth visiting.
title: Go and see!

body: We assumed that this would be a poor, tourist designed experience, but were delighted. Impossible to be cynical about 50 baby elephants looking very healthy and unfettered, all charging in from the open terrain to get funnel fed extra milk and forage! Grandstand viewing platform. Still don't quite understand where all these orphans come from, but the standard of care and commitment to the welfare of the animals is obvious. Don't miss it if you are staying near Udawale.
title: Elephant Transit Home, Udawale Park

body: That is the sentence on the only sign visible to the crowd, an honourable sentiment. Except there is no staff to enforce it, and visitors' behaviour is absolutely disrespectful. The poor elephants are forced to parade, in order to eat, in front of a disgusting crowd with crying babies, groups laughing at the top of their voices, a constant chatter that gave me a headache, and people taking pictures with flash - in plain sunlight. I hope you are ashamed of yourseleves. It felt like being at the circus. By the end, I was crying with rage. The elephants are re-introduced into the wild when they grow up, and should be used to nature, not constant loud noises every time they are hungry. PLEASE, hire 2 or 3 security guards to enforce silence, and throw out the disrespectful crowd. Increase the ticket price if you must, I would gladly pay double for a better experience. This project should have the animals' welfare at its core, not the pleasure of tourists.
title: "The jungle is silent, you too be silent"

body: If you're doing the safari, then you should definitely make sure to try and stop off here as part of your trip. You can watch *loads* of baby elephants during their feeding time - very cute. Definitely worth a visit if you're in the vicinity and the timings match up - and you'll only need an hour or so maximum here.
title: Well worth stopping off here alongside safari

body: This was magical! Amazing to see elephant orphans all being cared for so well by the Elephant Transit Home before released again into the wild. Wonderful to watch them during feeding time. Don't miss the museum onsight and the chance to donate to this great work.
title: Don't miss!

body: Would absolutely recommend a trip to the transit home - at feeding times. We went the day after our safari on our way to Ella. Go just before midday to watch around 30 baby and young elephants being fed their lunch. It’s an incredible experience! Although there’s no commentary, I overheard that they currently care for 48 baby elephants. We also saw many grown elephants that can’t be re-released for various health reasons (one had a prosthetic leg) so they will care for them for life. Brilliant rehab/sanctuary doing important conservation work.
title: Holiday highlight and a good cause

body: An absolute must for all those lucky enough to visit the area. Good viewing platform to observe these lovely creatures. Watching baby elephants run to their feed is a memory I will treasure.
title: Wonderful, very engaging.

body: The main and possibly only thing to do here is to see the elephant feeding time at the camp. It's a great view of the amazing elephants, feeding times are 915 12 and 330.Theres a modest exhibition also onsite. Worth a visit if you're not going to be seeing elephants elsewhere otherwise save it for an elephant safari.
title: If you aren't going on an elephant safari, check it out.

body: A place that cares about elephants!In previous reviews, people have stated there's cruelty to the elephants. I think people are seeing what they want to see, and think the worst. If you watch carefully, the man with the stick hits the ground by the elephant a majority of the time to move the elephants on. If people had taken the time to go to the information centre, they'd have read about the thickness of the elephant skin, which means the stick would not hurt them. It also states that elephants, especially the infant ones are greedy and are just like naughty, greedy children and will continue to drink the milk and not let others have some. The Sri Lankans are Buddhists, they love animalsPlease watch carefully, and praise the good work they're doing here.
title: Brilliant place!

body: You can see the elephants eating 4 times a day. We made it in time to see them having lunch. It’s a great sight to watch, especially the little calves messing around and rolling in the mud puddles. Definitely worth a trip if you’re going to the Udawalawe National Park.
title: Wonderful to watch them eating lunch

body: Little elephants are under care of best people and doctors. Best time to visit they are feeding time. Enjoyable.
title: Best Charity Program

body: We went on a Friday morning and were surprised to find there were more locals and schoolchildren here than tourists, which was nice to see. Whilst you do see the baby elephants being fed and they are very cute, I had expected a lot of information about how they find the babies to help them, the process to ensure they integrate with the herds, success numbers, the impact they are having on the population etc - there was none of this at all. You are left with just a couple of out of date promotion boards. I also was uncomfortable with the man with the stick. He didn’t seem overly aggressive, but again some information about why this was necessary and why there wasn’t a better way would have been helpful
title: Not what I expected and could be so much better

body: We enjoyed this place. Very reasonable entrance fee compared to most places in SL (500 SLR). All the young elephants come running up with their trunks up and their mouths open. There is also an older elephant hanging around with a prosthetic leg which is pretty amazing.
title: Great place to visit at feeding time

body: Before coming to Sri Lanka I had read quiet a lot online about how some places advertised themselves as orphanages but really were quiet cruel to the animals and had decided it’s best to avoid these places. I had not heard of this orphanage before coming to Udawalawe, it was recommended by our homestay host, I quickly googled this orphanage and read mixed reviews I decided to visit seeing as it was just down the road from my homestay. The baby elephants were allowed in to the area in twos to get fed, when they were done feeding they were directed to move onto an area with some branches/leaves for them to eat, if they didn’t move on as they should the man directing them would hit them with a stick, I understand that when dealing with a heard of young elephants you need to keep order however I personally found it upsetting to see him hit some of them, there was a few very young ones that were flinching from him I didn’t like this. In the end I left before the elephants were finished being fed. My boyfriend who had also come with me felt that the keeper needed to be strict with them to keep them in order which I understand I just did not like seeing such young elephants being hit.
title: Upsetting experience

body: We saw the feeding of the young elephants. Especially the adult elephant with a prothesis (was obviously cought in a trap with wire) was impressive. Its good to see that Zoo Cologne gave support to this park.
title: So cute the little one's

body: We stopped off here on our tour. The whole feeding process was very professional and smooth and ever so cute. Worth a stop.
title: Worth a stop

body: This was a early morning visit at feeding time for the baby elephants, we were pleased to see that a local class of young children were there for the experience too. The baby elephants were so cute coming in small groups to be fed until there were about 50 of them. You cannot interact with the elephants here as they are released to the wild when older and this was one of the main reasons we visited.Highly recommended.
title: Just fantastic.

body: It is great to have these beautiful animals looked after and the park is wonderful for them. I worry about them being hearded up to see the tourists - to make us happy and to make us feel as if we have contributed. The sticks and the hitting were done to keep them in place for our benefit.I would rather no one visited, we all contribute to this treatment. The carers are really there for the right reasons - but are we?
title: Beautiful Elephants - big hit and hearded so we can see them?

body: This is a must to do whilst here. I think I had a big smile on my face for over an hour whilst watching all the babies come in for their milk. Cost around £2 each but would have paid much more for the experience. Fantastic.
title: So So Cute

body: Please note that you will only be allowed inside during the milk feeding time (9am, 12pm & 3pm).'Namal' the three legged elephant will be fed first then follows the rest of the little ones.There's a clip/mini documentary on YouTube by BBC Earth on how Namal lost his leg. It was nice watching these baby elephants being fed, playing and doing their own thing.However, I would not agree with the place being accused for elephant abuse. Non of the elephants were chained nor looked unhappy. Definitely worth a visit if you're in Udawalawe.
title: Baby Elephants

body: I'm unsure about certain reviews having been left which have been defined as these animals being abused... while I did see a couple of short taps of a stick and while this is never very nice, given the volume of elephants to be fed, this was necessary. There are lots of elephants to see here. We benefited from having a highly organised Intrepid tour guide (Thilantha) who made sure we got there in plenty of time and even gave us recommendations as to the best area of the platform to sit on. Seeing all these elephants rush excitedly towards the feeding pens is just something everyone needs to see once. Very very cute and they are also hilarious as they do try and get extra milk. There is a large space for them to go and eat leaves and wallow around in a waterhole just after. It's so nice knowing that these elephants have been given a second chance after being abandoned by their mothers. They apparently feed 3 times a day and they all look healthy therefore not symptomatic of any "abuse" as described in other reviews. Loved it.
title: A beautiful experience watching elephants feed and play

body: Completely over-rated for the price we paid. We spent less than 30 minutes here. The place was over crowded so you had to stand on top toes to see the elephants.The Experience of seeing baby elephants was magical to begin with, then became apparent that the orphans were poked with sticks. One baby was clearly very hungry still and kept trying to return to the feeding point, the keeper took a stick and repeatedly poked it into the side of his head and hit his feet. The entire crowd reacted negatively to this, however sadly this seems the cold hard reality of Sri Lanka. Animals are mistreated and used as a tourist trap to make money. Although it’s wonderful to see the animals, it’s heartbreaking to see them treated this way. If they can hurt the babies in front of hundreds of people, I dread to think what happens behind the scenes. Don’t waste your money here! I will be writing to our travel agent on my return to let them know what this place is really like, as this should not be advertised to tourists as a ‘must visit’. I would never fund a trip like this again!
title: Over-rated & Animal abuse!

body: DO NOT VISIT HERE! At first when all the baby elephants came out it was so cute but then a man with a white stick appeared and started hitting the baby elephants on their legs, back and even on their heads. The force in which he hit them with was highly unnecessary, you could hear it from 50m away where we were sat. He was making them move away from the milk once they had had the tiniest bit but continued to hit some of the tiny babies repeatedly even after they had moved away. Lots of them cowered from him, I dread to think what goes on behind the scenes if they treat them like that in front of an audience. I could not believe what I saw. Please please DO NOT go here I was close to tears and had to leave.
title: Animal abuse

body: If you have even the slightest soft corner for elephants, this place will bowl you over. Imagine a herd of baby elephants frolicking in front of you. We visited at feeding time ie 12 noon. The viewing platform was already quite full, but we managed to find ourselves a good vantage point. Definitely worth visiting if you are anywhere in the vicinity.... or even a couple of hours away.
title: Cuteness personified

body: So many baby elephants! Watching them at feeding time would make the most miserable of humans smile! Very good program which introduced these babies back into the wild! Cheap entry.
title: Melts your heart.

body: Had the most amazing hour or so watching feeding time. We got there early and it was really busy with locals as school holidays. Highly recommend.
title: Highlight of my visit to Sri Lanka

body: It did get very busy so getting there beforehand is a good option.The elephants you can tell are well looked after and its hilarious watching them excitedly wave their trunks while running to get the milk. They do so in small groups. There was one who was adamant they wanted more milk and kept trying to pretend they had not had some milk and was a different elephant.. ts worth going into the information center after the elephants.
title: Just amazing

body: Such a worthwhile thing to seeVery cheap to get in and nice to see 60 plus elephants getting fedWould definitely recommend
title: Elephant feeding

body: i like the baby elephants in the elephant orphanage they took me safely to their with a safari cab i like it so much
title: So nise

body: This was a very pleasant surprise. We went to the 6:00 pm feeding, and watched about 40 baby elephants trotting out for their feeding, with their bellowing cries. The youngest were bottle fed (gulping it down rapidly) while the others had funnels. The big surprise was that the viewing platform was full of locals. I was thrilled to see this was educational not just for tourists, but for the local population to learn how to coexist with the elephants. Wonderful organization.
title: Overload of cuteness

body: Having been on safari and seen so man at wild elephants we were unsure of whether to go, as we had an extra day at udawalawe and couldn’t afford another safari we thought we would give it a go. We were very pleasantly surprised! Most of the elephants don’t live there, but come in at certain times of the day to be fed milk. It’s very cute to see them run in from the jungle to get there feed, from tiny elephants only a few months old to older ones that are around 3. There is also a great information museum that tells you about there work, do make sure you check the times as it is only open just before feeding time is due.
title: Cute young elephants!

body: Lots of elephants to see during feed time. We were there for the 12pm feed and could see lots of elephants from babies to adults having a feed of milk and leaves. There was also a bull elephant with a prosthetic limb which was nice to see. Strongly suggest a recorded commentary in English and local language so visitors know the story behind the transit house and also during the feeding session.
title: Commentary required

body: At 9, 12, 15 and 18.00, baby elephants get their milk... recommended to be 15minutes in advance. Not much to say, except that is extremely cute to see!! I think they have about 30 to 40 elephants, in my opinion well treated. Very nice little touristical activity. Interesting to know: if you go a little but further on the road (in the direction of the national park), you get a view on which nice land the baby elephants can play).
title: Cute little elephants

body: This is a fantastic Conservation project. It was a delightful experience to see these beautiful baby elephants being fed. The young elephants, which live wild in the Park, are fed several times a day with milk containing necessary supplements. Some of these elephants are tiny - maybe only a couple of months old. Although they are in the same group as the others they are too small and easy for the larger ones to push aside - so they are fed differently and individually. We paid 500 LKR for entrance fee Which is about £2.50 small priced to pay for good cause.
title: Born Free

body: I was relieved to read that this was noted as being a responsible orphanage that does what it says (ie rescue orphaned elephants for release back into wild). There are other places in which elephants are bred for display. We watched the morning feed which was a delight and the whole place seemed well run.
title: Great way to see elephants

body: The elephant transit home is a small facility on the border of the national park which cares for orphan elephants until they are ready to be released into the wild. You watch from behind a barrier as the elephants follow the keeper into the compound and eagerly await their turn to receive milk. It is lovely to see, and elephants look adorable and you see them playing and being mischievous. As a family we all enjoyed it and the feeding times are about 3 hours apart and the visit takes around an hour or so, there is a small visitor centre too.
title: Lovely to see the young elephants!

body: A visit to the elephant transit home is a must for any animal lover. The orphaned elephants are looked after until they are able to be released back out into the wild. It is not possible to see the elephants out in the jungle areas but you can see them being feed twice a day. All the elephants are bought into the feeding area and they keep you very entertain for about 45 mins. A great visit before moving on to Yala National Park.
title: An Elephant lovers dream!

body: You will see how these orphaned elephants get feed for about an hour. Don't expect to get close to the elephants, you must observe from a stand, but you see everything. Eventually these elephants go back into the wild.
title: Elephant Nursery

body: This place is a great way to spend an hour. The young elephants get fed a jug of milk each several times of day. The come running up to the milk bar pushing others out of the way. The workers are careful to ensure each elephant gets it's share and no more. The information centre is a bit old but informative with a short video which was interesting to watch prior to our safari into the park. In the grounds was a tree with two owls in a hole which was an extra treat.The ethics seemed good and it does seem the successfully release the elephants back into the park.
title: Baby elephants

body: The public were kept away from the elephants who were all youngsters rescued after they had been orphaned. They will all eventually be released into the wild- hence their limited contact with humans. A heartening place!
title: At last an ethical elephant sanctuary

body: As an animal lover I was dubious about visiting this orphanage from reading prior reviews. I was saddened by the number of little elephants that have been unfortunate to be orphaned but this sanctuary provides food and care for them while allowing them to live as free as possible. The reviews regarding sticks are in my opinion not correct. Some of the elephants are cheeky and try to get second helpings of milk and they are given a tap (not a hit!) on the bum to allow other elephants to feed. They are very cute too!
title: Not what I expected

body: I really can‘t understand the number of good reviews. We were just sad after the visit. We saw underfed baby elephants repeatedly hit with a stick because they were begging for some more milk. I’m no expert but that’s definitely not how you treat orphaned baby animals. I don’t want to know what happens when no tourists watch.But most of the audience seemed to have a really good laugh seeing this.
title: Don‘t go!

body: We enjoyed watching the elephants come up for their feeding. The babies getting their bottles was especially cute. Be prepared to have to stand amongst a jostling crowd.
title: Lovely elephants

body: This is a elephant transit home for baby orphan elephants and disabled elephants. They have milk feeding times 4 times a day. I have uploaded a photo of it along with the entrance fees. You are not allowed to touch or go near any of the baby elephants. The entire session lasts about 30 min. The elephants are fed milk with a funnel and tube / hose. after which the elephants go near the water hole and bath and play in it.
title: Check the feeding time before you visit I posted a image of it

body: Defnitely recommend going to watch the elephants being fed. There are about 40 elephants. Feeding is four times a day.
title: Eating elephants

body: 3 times a day 30-40 baby/young Elephants get their milk. It is really lovely to see the Elephants lining up for milk in a gentle way and to see the kind way the staff is taking care. So far more than 150 Elephants have been released into the Park which is right next doorThis is not a tourist place to play with the animals - this is real life where employees are making a real difference for these endangered animals.
