body: this is a place where the orphaned elephants go to then be released into he wild again theres a sign up that says its quiet in the jungle so be quiet ,but that wasnt happening when we were there with alot of children! however i think it was good that you couldnt get near them etc feed them or anything like that worth going to see
title: interesting

body: We attended the 9am feeding time and saw so may baby elephants. You need to get there fairly early as the tickets are all hand written so takes time to actually get through the gates and the venue is a haven for school parties. The is an excellent way to spend about 45 minutes observing these wonderful animals.
title: Feeding time!

body: The milk feeding times are 9am, noon, 3pm and 6pm. There are three rows of flat concrete stairs to sit on. If you are in the front at 9am it could be pretty hot as the sun comes round and the shade goes.Young elephants are fed milk and older ones fed leaves on branches.There is no commentary, you simply watch the elephants feed then they go out of sight. They do some good work here. If you don’t go in the information centre you won’t learn anything about the rehabilitation.Shame there are no prices on the goods in the gift shop. There is a small supermarket opposite which has normal prices.
title: Lots of elephants!

body: There are 4 feeding times a day during which you can see the elephants in a group. A bit voyeuristic but there is no contact between visitors and elephants to protect them. The cost is 500 rupees for foreigners which is good value and the funds are clearly put to good use. A small museum and information centre describing the work of the sanctuary is also on site. Worth a visit.
title: Enjoyable!

body: Unlike some other elephant places in Sri Lanka, the elephants here are genuinely cared for, so it is worth visiting especially at feeding time. There is a small museum which is also interesting.
title: So lovely to see the baby elephants

body: A lovely setting seeing the young and baby elephants waiting at the gate for their turn to be fed by the keepers. Once they had finished their milk they came nearer the viewing area which is shaded to eat the branches and leaves left for them. It is lovely to watch them interact with each other .
title: Baby elephant

body: I will never forget the sight of the young elephants dashing to the 'canteen' to get their milk. a wonderful worthwhile project.
title: absolutely amazing

body: So great to see Oprah baby elephants being looked after, the milk feeding times are 9-12-3 and 6. Get there early to get a good seat so you can see this amazing little elephants
title: Beautiful

body: We visited here in early February for the 3 pm feed. The feeds start promptly at the allotted time.It is wise to arrive at least 15 minutes before hand as this gives you time to choose where to stand or sit. If you have small children this is important as they need to be on the front row to see what is going on. The viewing area is rather like an old football stand. It is terraced and covered so you get protection from the rain or sun. From the stands you look across a fenced area and at one end there is a feeding station where elephants who have not been weaned are given milk. Small elephant calves drink from large containers and the larger elephants take their milk via a tube. Fodder in the form of leaves on small twigs and small branches are spread out on the ground. You can watch elephants stripping the leaves and feeding themselves. The elephants are effectively carolled. The smaller elephants are fed first. The age range of the elephants are approximately 4/6 months up to 6 years. There are a few older adult elephants who cannot be released back into the wild but these tend to stay in the background under cover. There are well over 30 elephants to see here.Meal times are social times for elephants. We were rather surprised at how orderly and well behaved the elephants were. Yes their is is some queue jumping and the little calves will run rather than walk to get their food but it is well managed and quite delightful to see. It took me back lunch times for youngsters in the school canteen when they were full off chatter, excited to be getting their lunch and not wanting to sit or stand still!You also get a good idea of the physiological development of elephants at different ages. The very young calves have quite a lot of ‘baby hair’ on the head and down the spine. The elephants will congregate in small groups, keeping close to each other. We observed some interesting behaviour of elephants using their trunks to massage or stroke other elephants (see photo). In one case a very young calf was laying on the floor and some slightly older elephants came up to it and stroked it belly and side. It seemed that the elephant lying down just didn't want to get up to eat, whilst the older elephants were urging it to do so knowing that if it did not get in the queue soon all the folder would have been taken. Occasionally you will see egrets on the back of an elephant (see photo). You will probably see some of the bigger elephants wearing a leather collar. The collar is for tracking purposes. Elephants with collars we were told were soon to be released into the wild. Comment has been made on this site about the elephant herdsmen carrying sticks and using them to control the herd. The sticks they carry are relatively short, say about 2 feet long, and are more like twigs than sticks. I never saw these twigs/sticks being used as a weapon. Very occasionally when a group of 3 or more elephants needed some separation the sticks might be used by giving a gentle prod to separate one or more elephants. You see this sort of behaviour in UK cattle markets when cows need to be separated or guided. It is not cruel or punitive. It is just a method to keep separation and to ensure the herdsmen do not get trodden on or squashed in the melee. The feeding lasts about 20/40 minutes and it provides an opportunity to take some lovely photos. This activity makes for a good video if your camera does videos. People who are watching are not allowed to touch or pet the animals.
title: A must see place if you are i interested in the rearing of elephants

body: These take orphans and young elephant into the park, and bring them in at night for some milk (and cookies lol) before being let out to the park at night. The animals all queue up at the gate ready and trumpeting to get their milk and we were priveleged to watch them being fed.
title: Good Cause

body: We arrived here for the 9am feeding. It was lovely to see the elephants here before we started our safari at Udawalawe (where we were lucky enough to see many more elephants). From what we saw they seemed to care for the elephants well, definitely worth a visit if in the area.
title: Worth a visit!

body: Reading about the different homes and orphanages we were a bit sceptical (as animal lovers) however the reviews of this place are almost all good so we ‘dared’ to go. The place is pretty straightforward: you sit, watch and be quiet, while the elephants are fed. The entrance is way too cheap for tourists but of course you can donate if you want ;-) the feeding is truly winderful to see but also brings up questions like how far do we interfere with nature? Interesting questions for during diner. For me it was a bit too much after visiting the national park, for my wife it was amazing...
title: A good place (as it seems)

body: Lovely to see these orphaned elephants cared for in a superb way and re introduced into the wild when old enough.Definitely go at feeding time 9am 12md 3pmPlenty of room on the viewing platform, a little distance away from the feeding station, so does not disturb the elephants.Great to see the tiny ones running over to feed!Very interesting information facility on the life of the elephant.Definitely worth a visit.
title: Great work!

body: Make sure your guide knows when feeding times are. We arrived in time for the elephants 9am breakfast. A well managed and wildlife success story. There were over 30 orphaned elephants in the transit home and we spent an hour or so there.
title: Definitely worth a visit

body: An absolute must visit, the sight of the baby, and young elephants coming in for their milk will stay with me for a long time, if not forever. Found it quite emotional.
title: Awesome!

body: If you are in the area, this is definitely worth a visit. Get there for one of their regular feeding times (we hear it's 5) to watch the young elephants. Takes about 30 mins and is a lot of fun to watch. You can also make donations to help this organisation rehabilitate these baby elephants back into the wild.
title: A wonderful place for all ages

body: A definite must see is the feeding time here. Entry is 500 rupees which goes to support their work. Gates are open about 30 mins before the babies come in for feeding. Best views are probably between the middle and slightly to the right of the covered viewing area.We arrived at 2:30 for the 3pm feeding and had no trouble finding a good place to watch.Some of the babies are just a few months old and very cute. We saw between 35 and 45 elephants there. The feeding itself takes about 20 minutes as the elephants are let up to the feeding station in batches.
title: Dozens of baby elephants

body: The first thing to say is that this is not like those elephant places in India and Thailand where the animals are chained up. This is a well run enterprise supported by The Born Free Trust. When we visited last week there were 52 elephants from a few months to 7 years old, they are re introduced into the wild or into reserves when they reach 7 years. Some were wearing collars containing a micro chip so that they could be tracked and their progress monitored following their release.To see them queuing up and then rushing to the feeding area was an experience I shan't forget in a hurry, the children watching absolutely loved it. Please go and support them, you can make a donation and also act as a sponsor for one of them.Highly Recommended.
title: A Really Lovely Experience

body: We went to the 6 pm feeding and it was so lovely to see so many happy little elephants being well cared for. We'd avoided several tourist elephant facilities while in Sri Lanka but this one seemed to genuinely be about caring for the elephants and we were happy to see this was so when we got there. The elephants are kept at a distance and there are signs up explaining why you cant touch them and why you shouldn't ask to. You get a lot more than you pay for, and there is an exhibition area with more information that sadly was closed at the 6 pm feeding so go earlier in the day if you'd like to see this.
title: happy baby elephants

body: A brilliant centre which is doing excellent work to protect elephantsA must see place if you are in the areaFeeding times are 9. 12. 3. 6 o’clock Don’t miss out on the information centre after you have seen the feeding. It is fascinating and has lots of easy to read displays
title: Fantastic to watch feeding time

body: These people are really doping very good work! So nice to see how the orphan elephants are fed and trained to go back to the jungle as the reach 5 years. Please leave a donation for the good word when you visit this transit camp
title: Lovely

body: After the usual chaos of getting tickets and getting into the Transit Home (I really don't understand why this is so difficult everywhere in Sri Lanka - always a scrum) we sat on a terraced area where everyone could get a good view of feeding time.The elephants are allowed into the feeding area a few at a time and I suppose it took around 40 minutes for them all to be fed.Some of the orphans are very small and some look like teenagers but all are clearly well looked after.We went to the evening (6pm) feeding session (as part of our tour) and therefore unfortunately the education centre was closed (which we have liked to have visited. If you want to see this go during one of the day time (9am, 12 noon and 3pm) feeding sessions.
title: Excellent to see how these orphan elephants are being looked after

body: Do many orphaned baby elephants of all sizes.Took about an hour to feed them all.They were let into the feeding area in an orderly manner so they were all fed.Once all were fed, they were led off to the night paddock.Was great to watch the interactions of the elephants.
title: Baby elephant feeding

body: A well presented display naturally done and a worthy cause. Staff looking after these orphaned elephants obviously enjoy their work and do a great job. Even watching from a 'grandstand' the experience is top grade, a delight for children.
title: So many happy baby elephants :)

body: The ETH cares for orphaned baby elephants until they are old enough to be released into the Udawalawa reserve. Feeding times are every 3 hours. Visitors sit on concrete tiers to watch the process. 500 rupees per person and all in good cause.
title: Elephants in a line

body: This is a very nice place and for what it costs, you get lot more than what you ask for. Ensure that you have this on your itenerary if you are ever visiting Uda Walawe area.
title: Absolute must visit if you are visiting Udawalawe

body: touristic but nice location. Especially a place to go for children. Do not forget to have a look into the museum, where Dilmah Tea Foundation as a sponsor, obviously did a good job by explaining all about the functioning of the elephant. Good place to stay dry in monsoon time. The feeding place is also covered so that you can take all your time to watch the little elephants getting their milk bottles, and after that, the bigger ones as well.
title: very touristic site

body: Feeding time here was great fun with elephants of different ages coming up in small groups for lunch. Slightly twee but good fun and many repatriated elephants have since bred
title: Good fun and good cause

body: We booked the tour from a local travel organizer in Hikkaduwa (Jayantha tours, +97 774043831). Owner Mr. K.M.G. Jayantha is fluent in english and very friendly and reliable. Visit to the Elephant Transit Home was part of our visit the the Udawalawe nationall park as they are next to each other. The feeding takes place only a few times in a day so try to organize your visit to the ETH and to Udawalawe park in order not to miss the feeding. There is a smallish visit center at ETH that gives information about elephants and the purpose of the ETH. The feeding is next to the visit center and in the shades. The big number of elephants that come to the feeding was quite a surprise to us. Definitely worth the visit - consider donating some extra money for the ETH.
title: See milk feeding of wild elephants

body: Had an interesting visit here. Good work being done and an interesting information centre too. Worth a look
title: Very informative

body: It was a great experience to see the young elephants coming for their feed. They were adorable running up to get in line for their milk. We were surprised at just how many of them there was, and after feeding on milk they come and eat some leaves from branches which is fun to watch. Arrive about 15 minutes before feeding time to get a good view of it all. Not a lot else to do (the small museum wasn’t even open when we went), so make sure to go for a feeding time. We went at 6pm.
title: cute baby elephants!!

body: You must make sure that you get there at the feeding times which are every half hour and last for about 30 minutes. The elephants will line up in front of you and you can see them feeding. However you can't feed them yourself though you can donate money to make their life better.
title: Don't miss

body: It was wonderful to see all these elephants especially the babies during feeding time. There are 4 feeding times per day for the public - 9.00 am, 12 .00 noon, 3.00 & 6.00 pm. The entrance fee is 500 SL rupees.
title: Feeding Time

body: Went to watch the 6pm feeding time for the elephants who arrive in small groups. They clearly all know where to head for their evening milk. Most of the very tiny ones disappeared to be fed behind the feeding station but one slightly bigger one, still very tiny, seemed not to have an idea how to feed from leaves etc. I guess it will learn eventually. We witnessed no cruelty here at the ETH and are delighted that we were able to lend our support to this worthy organisation.
title: Supporting a good cause in the hope of elephants being returned to the wild.

body: Definitely an hour well spent. Make sure you arrive for a feeding time of 9am and every 3 hours until 6pm. Otherwise there's not much happening.
title: Fun visit

body: ETH is run by the Born Free Foundation and is attached to, but separate from Uda Walawe National Park, just a short way from the Park entrance which involves a lovely drive over a reservoir causeway. The feeding times are 9am,12noon,3pm and 6pm. As we were at the end of our tour and had already been in Yala NP, we just made a stop off to see the 12 noon feeding. A lot of people we spoke with seemed to have done an early morning visit to the Park and attending the feeding afterwards, which I think is a really good combination. Entry is not expensive and there is an excellent viewing area, with seating, but you are unable to have any contact with the elephants who are perhaps some 20 - 50 yards away. The place is very well organised and it was lovely to see the queue of about 50 elephants waiting for their call, small ones at the front, as they are let in to the feeding station in 3s & 4s. They are first given milk, the very small ones from a large babys' bottle then move on to a large pile of branches and leaves (jackfruit?) There are elephants of all sizes, they are kept here til around 5 years old, then let into the wild. The bigger ones had collars, which enable them to be monitored once they leave. The whole session only lasts about 30 minutes, then as if by magic they turn round and head back into the Park; that is until the next feeding time. A magical and unmissable experience
title: Watch elephants feeding and support a good cause

body: Arrived at 3pm for afternoon feed. Lovely to watch the baby elephants and also injured ones being fed and looked after. Particularly impressed with the large elephant which had a prosthetic leg!
title: Baby Elephants Aah!

body: Several times a day the orphaned and rescued elephants walk to the feeding station and get either milk if they are small or other food if they are larger. There's a big viewing area and it all seems fairly natural. A cheap bit of entertainment suitable for all the family as it's not too long and there is shelter from the heat.
title: A good half hour activity

body: The Elephant Transit Home is well worth a visit - it is only open at 3 times of the day for the public to watch the feeding. It’s an amazing sensory experience hearing the trumpeting of many elephants of all sizes demanding their milk. It’s also a wonderful charity looking after orphaned and injured elephants, and releasing them back into the wild once they are recovers or old enough - definitely worth supporting.
title: Wonderful!

body: There are four feeding times, we went at 3 PM and the place was packed, I found the price very reasonable, even a bit too low, to be honest. You can see the elephants close up but not interact with them, which is great, as they are released into the park when they are about 5 years old and don't need any unnecessary human interaction. The rangers do occasionally "hit" them with a wooden stick, but it's really only to keep them in line, as even the small ones are very large and potentially dangerous - no "violence" involved at all! The Information centre contains lots of useful Information about the elephants, the grounds are also home for many birds (we saw a sleeping owl and a beautiful woodpecker).
title: A good place to see baby elephants close up

body: Really loved this place Feeding time is about 30 mins but is fab to see All the elephants various ages and size running in for their milk Done trying to rejoin the queue for more bring gently moved along with a wooden stick Could have watched it all day The whole place seemed great and the museum also taught me things I didn't know about elephants
title: Elephants for the wild

body: This is a wonderful place to visit, seeing the baby elephants and the disabled elephants running towards the feeding station is a sight to behold! Other people have mentioned maltreatment but we saw none of that, the keepers are simply corralling rowdy junior elephants.We went to the 12 noon feeding, arriving 15 mins early allowed us to get a good front seat view. It lasts around 30 minutes. The seats are concrete steps and there is sunshade. Very well worth the 500 SLR entrance fee. We also made a donation for milk.
title: Keeping orphaned baby wild elephants wild!

body: This was one of my top experiences in Sri Lanka! Baby elephants were so funny and cute! The tap on the bum that I read in some reviews wouldn't even hurt a human, let alone an elephant. They do that to naughty elephants who try to come back for more milk. It's clear that the elephants love the humans who take care of them and don't appear to be the least frightened by them. The museum is also very interesting. Definitely worth a visit!
title: I could stay there all day long!

body: When this program was started it maybe had good intentions of caring for orphaned elephants. Today, I saw baby elephants being hit by their handlers with sticks. Some of the elephants cried out, whilst others were silent and simply knew where they had to go - presumably after months or years of this kind of treatment.Why were they hit? To make them move so the tourists could get a better view of them. I felt sick.Many of these elephants are orphaned due to human behaviour. It saddens me to see that the very program claiming to protect and nurture these beautiful animals seems to be part of the problem. And by being there, so was I.
title: Human behaviour at its worst

body: Nice to see that young orphaned elephants are nursed and then released into the wild when they van fend for themselves again. The park had 56 elephants when we visited. They feed the elephants 3 or 4 times a day, we watched it at 3 pm. There is an elephant museum that is also worth a visit, where you can learn lots about elephants.
title: Elephant orphanage and museum worth a visit

body: Compare to Pinawalla which is a Tourist business this one is really respectful for the elephant and they have a program of realising the elephant in the wild when they are strong enough.So I would recommand this one more than any other!
title: Quiet and peaceful

body: Just visited the elephant orphanage to see the feeding. The feeds happen every 3 hours from 6am to 6pm & entry cost is 500Rs/person. Lots of baby elephants turned up for the feed, great to see them so close.
title: Baby elephants

body: The elephants seem very well cared for. True that the carers give them them the odd tap on the bum with a stick, but people who are claiming these animals are absurd perhaps are naive to the realities of controlling large animals. This doesn’t feel like the typical tourist trap where the elephants are exploited, they are released into the park at 5 years old and were happy, playing with their carers and wrestling with them for milk
title: Wonderful

body: No glitz, or hard sell, just a great place to watch the young elephants being fed (twice a day - check the times). Well worth it.
title: Genuinely beautiful

body: Our family was traumatized by this horrible experience. They don't really care about the animals. They hit them and don't care for the babies. Not recommended for children or anyone. Tell the manager if you see any abuse.
title: Terrible place

body: It is crazy to see some of the bad reviews here. The elephants obviously love the handlers. Yes, they tap them with a stick, but they are baby elephants that are quite sneaky and mischievous as they try to sneak back for more food.Someone wrote this would be shut down in the west... Ha! The way elephants are treated here is far better than how elephants are treated in Western Zoos.Definitely worth stopping in. Takes about 30 minutes.
title: Fantastic Orphanage

body: We visited the Elephant Transit Centre yesterday and were impressed with how they care for so many orphaned and injured elephants on such tight budgets. It’s an important local enterprise and also aims to educate visitors. I’d recommend visiting the education centre first where they explain all about the physiology of elephants, provide interesting facts for younger kids and also highlight the importance of protecting species. It is true that they hit the elephants with wooden sticks, but it’s sparing and only to direct them towards the feeding station (and to keep away the cheeky ones that sneak back for more). At first our kids were a little shocked, but we explained that the elephants have skin that’s 2-3cm thick and the sticks aren’t very big. They are very cute & it would be easy to forget that they’re dangerous and wild animals which are being cared for. There would be no feasible way to feed up to 70 young elephants if they weren’t herded. It could also put the rangers in real danger. Afterwards we spoke to a ranger and he explained that there is no other way and if they can’t control them they wouldn’t be able to feed them all. And in reality, without this centre, most of the orphaned and injured juvenile elephants would die. The elephants at this centre don’t give rides and you can’t interact with them, as they aim to release them all into the wild when they mature sufficiently. It’s definitely worth waiting until the end of the feeding session, when they clear the feeding area and lead out an adult which has been fitted with a prosthetic leg. It’s amazing to see and the rangers all made a fuss of it. It was also really great to see that some of the older elephants are fitted with trackers and are now free to roam the National Park. They often choose to come back for a period whilst they adjust to life beyond the transit centre.Worth a visit, but perhaps they should provide more info about why they herd the elephants so children don’t get upset.
title: Worth going to the education centre before seeing the feeding

body: This is a true orphanage which releases orphaned elephants back into the national park. The elephants can be a bit unruly and excited at feeding time and keeping them under control at feeding time can be a noisy affair. Your entrance fee is used to fund the elephants. Don't this place get confused with there is only one "orphaned" elephant there the rest are privately owned and are captive and chained for elephant rides.
title: Must see place...(don't go to Pinnewala near Kandy - it's not an "orphanage")

body: We are a family with children who have traveled in dozens of countries and visited many animal, including elephant, orphanage facilities. This was by far the worst. It is shocking that it is supported by the Government of Sri Lanka. The elephant handlers are abusive to the elephants. Several elephants were hit harshly and hard, one directly on its trunk and several small-baby ones were also hit hard. Our children started crying and asked to leave. The staff was totally unresponsive and essentially shrugged off our feedback as not a big deal. After repeated requests, the manager said they would train their staff better. I would avoid this place and certainly do not bring young children. Our teenager was also outraged, as we were.
title: Terrible facility. Would be shut down in the West.

body: We were really excited to support orphan elephants and see them being fed. Our 3 kids couldn’t wait! Unfortunately this turned out to be horrible because the people taking care of the elephants repeatedly hit them very hard with a huge stick (across the face and on their bodies) when the elephants wanted more food or just didn’t move in the direction the men wanted. We were horrified and our children started crying (even our teenagers!) and we walked out and went to talk to the park ranger who laughed at our crying children and said that the men do their best. He did promise to talk to the men about being gentler with the animals. Please don’t support this activity with your money and if you do go and see the elephants being hit, talk to the ranger. He should know that tourists don’t want to support animal abuse!
title: Horrible! Don’t go and support this!

body: This reserve is fantastic. Make sure you show up at 9am to see the baby elephants get fed. Only 500rupees/ person... About $3.50. Totally worth it!!
title: Amazing to see

body: Worth a visit if you ensure it is feeding time. 9.00am is one time and it was great to see some 40 young elephants fed by the staff. The feeding takes about 30 minutes and this is the main attraction. The information centre is okay and gives some basic introductory information about elephants.The centres aim is to rear the young elephants and then reintroduce them to the wild - into the national park next door.
title: Visit at feeding time.

body: Brilliant. Just wish there had been a guide telling us a little bit more about the elephants. Good information centre though.
title: Definitely worth a visit

body: I went there for the evening feeding session with my girlfriend on the night before we had a jungle safari in Udawalawa and were both left seriously upset and frustrated at what we had seen, and put our money to fund.From the moment we entered all we saw was numerous men walking around a number of visibly scared elephants and whacking them with sticks until the elephants screamed in pain and moved where the men were requesting.Unable to watch the blatant abuse we left after under a minute and requested our money back, which we were denied.When we tried to reason with the site manager as to why the practices were so wrong and disturbing he simply laughed and proclaimed "they are wild animals, how else are we going to control them" and then started attempting to justify their actions by asking if we think it is any better in zoos or circuses to which we replied that we do not go to zoos or circuses for that exact reason.He then went on to say that we do not know what happens behind closed doors in other orphanages, at which point we informed him that if he was willing to beat an animal with a stick in front of a crowded audience then there is no telling what they would do behind closed doors either.Avoid this place at all costs as it is somewhere which you will see adult elephants blatantly abused in front of you and then you will be laughed at for making a point about it.
title: Avoid at all costs

body: As an animal lover, I was concerned about visiting this place. The reports of hitting elephants with a stick are accurate, but seem slightly blown out of proportion. What I saw was light enough taps that it never ventured into remotely harmful. No elephants were in chains and they were all clearly happy. I’ve never seen animals so excited for feeding time!!! Don’t visit late at night. We were advised that the 6pm feeding was best. Wrong. It was so dark we struggled to see, couldn’t take pics and got ate up by mosquitoes.
title: Nice. Don’t go late.

body: This is an awesome place and for 700 rupees you get to see elephants that have been rescued, and are being rehabilitated to send back to the wild. It is a really sweet experience to watch baby elephants getting fed their milk by the handlers. They all look healthy and taken care of (we saw one with his leg in a cast), the place is really clean and it's heartwarming to see these beasts being cared for.
title: Super sweet experience

body: This place was a great addition to going to Udawalawe National Park. After seeing them in the wild, the Elephant Transit Home is a place for orphaned elephants to stay before being set into the wild. We made it just in time for feeding at 9am (definitely the best time to go is feeding time) with the entrance fee of 500LKR. All the money goes back to elephants, which made it so much more worth a visit. There are elephants with prosthetic legs and some of the baby elephants are only a few months old! The museum is very interesting, with facts you won’t get from your safari tour guide and the end gallery shows all the elephants that have been rehabilitated back into the wild! Very rewarding!! They are currently building a rod barrier around the feeding area which is hindering for photos, but still so worth a visit!
title: Great place to learn more about Sri Lanka’s national animal

body: Nice sanctuary to visit for an hour. Best to attend around feeding times. The elephants are feed for about 30/40 minutes and are then taken away. My only comment would be it would be nice to get a little bit closer to the elephants
title: Nice sanctuary to visit

body: We arrived just in time for the 12 noon feed. We were treated to a wonderful site of 40+ young elephants being fed with milk and leaves . Some were playful after feeding and a couple even performed in the water bath.All of the elephants were treated well and you are easily close enough to enjoy the spectacle without being intrusive. Across the road we had a nice lunch tooIt would be good if you could donate on their website as i would still like too.
title: Amazing and worthwhile hour

body: You need to arrive at one of the 3 feeding times. We were there for 9am, I’m not sure what the other times are. The young, some very young, elephant are let through a gate from the reserve a few at a time and given milk The encouraged to eat leaves. You view from a platform. It’s a lovely sight.
title: If you love elephants visit this!

body: The place is dedicated to taking care of baby elephants that are sick or orphan, untill they are old and steong enough to be released in the wild. You will have the chance to witness their feeding and see them play. If you are not yet a fan of these wonderful creatures, after a visit in Sri Lanka, I bet you will turn into one. And babies...well, babies will steal a piece of your heart for sure. You can adopt one for a day, mainly donate aome money that is used to their feeding. There is also an elephant museum on the premises, do not pass it by!!!
title: Tender encounter

body: This was not what I was expecting at all thought we would get up close with these beautiful animals but you were quiete away from them and you could only watch them bein* fed and cared for no reel interaction but would have missed it for the world babies from 3 months old
title: Good but not as good as told

body: Such an important asset to the park. And those baby elephants (sadly orphaned) and beyond cute. Make sure to visit at feeding time however... it’s 5 times a day And any guides will know the times. Do leave a donation, it’s a government organization and you’ll get a recipe but it costs a lot to care for these baby elephants in a natural environment so they can be released back into the wild
title: Loved this!

body: The elephant orphanage is a 10 minute drive from the Udawalawe National Park entrance. Feeding times are at 9AM, 12PM, 3PM, and 6PM. I would try and arrange your visit around these timings as I don't think there is much opportunity to see the orphans otherwise as they go back to their fields.It costs 500R(£2.50) for entry. There are toilets and stalls selling food/water/ice cream.We stayed for about 45 minutes watching the elephants be fed their milk (they were fed in order of size), eat their leaves and cool themselves off in the pond. I loved the elephant with the prosthetic leg, the hairiness of the tiniest elephants, and how they would all run away whenever a dog came nearby! Definitely get to the viewing platform about 15 minutes before so you can secure a good spot for taking photos.There is also a little information centre which provides a bit of background but you can do this in 5/10 minutes, the main attraction is the elephant feeding.The only thing I didn't like so much was that the trainers would punch/hit the elephants of they were being a bit naughty/over-excited.
title: The babies are so cute!

body: This place is less about you and being close to the elephants and more about the good it's doing for the elephants. The orphanage currently has over 30 elephants, and at the transit home you can visit at milking times four times a day, there is a viewing platform for visitors to observe the elephants at feeding time from a short distance which is a heart warming experience as you see just how many baby orphan elephants there are being looked after here. The transit house provides the elephants with the food and care they require before releasing elephants back into the wild where they are monitored, it really is a good cause and worth visiting.
title: Good cause

body: lots of rumours that you can bottle feed baby elephants - not true! Its a good experience and nice to see so many elephants from a distance - but you can't get near them. From a nature perspective I think that is a good thing - these elephants will be released back into the wild so human interaction should be limited. But the kids were disappointed because they were under the impression they could feed them
title: Lovely to go and see the orphaned elephants being cared for - but you can't get close or feed them

body: Visited after safari in Udawalawe National Park. Arrived just before 9am for morning feed. Already busy but plenty of room to view feeding area. Keepers allow the elephants in a couple at a time to avoid fights over milk. Once fed they all come to pond area in front of viewing platform to drink, bathe and play. A lovely 40 mind seeing teenage elephants down to very young babies. The home also cares for a couple of disabled elephants. Throughly recommended
title: Perfect mix of tourism and conservation

body: Don't miss this. Really, I mean it, don't miss it. For £2.50 you can spend a delightful half and hour seeing real genuine conservation work in progress. Supported by the Born Free Foundation you know it is sound. The price is embarrassingly low - please leave them a donation (get a receipt it says) and read the exhibition - very interesting. The WCs are terrible. You can buy ice cream and water across the road.
title: Excellent Conservation Project

body: My husband and I visited the elephant transit home last week. It was fabulous watching the little ones take the milk from the wildlife staff. They then went and wallowed in a watering hole. The babies played & wriggled around in the pond. Well looked after & the best thing is these animals will be released back into the wild if they can be.A wonderful project and simply delightful to enjoy such an intimate experience.Well worth a visit.
title: So Beautiful

body: Go for the safari in Udawalawe, easily better and closer views of elephants there! But the job they are doing here deserves a donation
title: Just a simple view from a platform

body: Having seen some of the negative reviews we were a bit unsure about this visit - however we did enjoy the visit and seeing all the baby’s at feeding time was great. Yes there was a guy with a stick but we did not think he used it in anger or without restraint. His job was clear and that was to ensure all the baby’s had the same opportunity for milk and this is no easy task dealing with over a dozen baby’s who have 2-3cm thick skin!! Admittedly It’s not a good look but as the baby’s keep coming back for more milk, and testing his patience in a cat and mouse game we felt they can’t be suffering 😳 The centre is a good thing for these animals and they certainly appear to care for them. The small information centre is also worth a visit to understand the important work they do.
title: Interesting visit

body: What an amazing place. They are an orphanage rehabilitating elephants however not using tourists to interact however to watch which I feel is a great idea. You watch the elephants come to feed and they have to take it in turns. Some of them come running from the pen to their milk overtaking and pushing others out of the way it's very funny to watch. They then play or eat greens in their group which is a joy to watch. It makes you smile watching the babies trying to stand fall and play. Very cute. It only lasts around half an hour however the entrance fee is only £2.50 and goes to a great cause. Definitely not to be missed. I did not a review reference them being beaten with a stick. They are tapped to keep in check from being naughty however they are big animals and in NO way did I see this as cruel.
title: Great fun !!!

body: If you love animals, this is a definite must do.The transit home has about 40 small Elephants in their care. Some are infants just a few months old. It is such a treat to see them all being herded to be fed Milk & then allowed to graze in the garden nearby. A really heart warming experience too see these animals queue up to get there share of Milk. You can even help by donating to the orphanage or go as far as taking over expenses for an Elephant till it is released. Hats off to the people who run the place, a remarkable initiative.
title: Very cute & heart warming

body: If you are in the area the Udawalawe Elephant Transit Home is not to be missed! It is one of very few elephant sanctuaries that actually appears to have the elephants welfare as a priority, and not making money from tourists at the elephants expense. There are no rides here, no bathing experiences, no painting - just observation.You pay 500 Rp and get to watch the elephants arrive for feeding 3 times a day. It lasts for about half an hour, and is very enjoyable to watch the young elephants (they are all orphans here, under the age of 4) come for milk. Some get cheeky and try to queue up twice but the keepers know the naughty ones and keep them in check. There is a small moat separating the elephant area from the tourists, but there is a large platform and everyone should get a good view. In my opinion this is how interacting with elephants should be; observing and enjoying from a distance. For 500 Rp it's a great way to spend half an hour.
title: How visiting elephants should be

body: Shelters baby elephants who are orphans. There are several of them looked after. You can watch them from the observation hut during feeding hours.
title: Wildlife

body: This place is a must see in Uda Walawe. The entree is 500SRP for adult foreigners, and it's nice to know that this money goes directly to support the elephant transit home and take care of the orphan elephants. They're so cute. It's very nice to see, doesn't take too long (30 minutes). We visited this place during feeding time at 18:00.
title: Must see - very cute

body: if you need to see baby elephants so colsely you must visit this place..you can see how they feeding..what a lovely place..baby elephants are so cute..
title: Amazing Place

body: Really enjoyed this and took a guide for an explanation of the park and how they work and care for the Elephants. Washed the elephants but didn't want to exploit the elephants by riding on them. A small outdoor but undercover elephant museum which is worth looking at.
title: Very Enjoyable

body: one of the most adorable scene I've ever seen. there are 20-30 baby elephants rushing to drink milk which is a wonderful scene. this place is more like a temporary care center instead of a orphanage.
title: Care center for baby elephants

body: Amazing work done by these people, it is wonderful that the babies have the chance which could have been lostOne thing did annoy me was that the man that moved the elephants along so the next lot could be fed locked them with a stick and I thought I more poke and I will poke you, I know they have thick skin but they are just babies trying it on for extra food, but other than that it was great
title: Great work

body: Got there to find many school children all looking at the same thing serveral small little elephants beening feed milk and one unforturate larger elephant who had lost part of his back leg due to a fire or landmine not shore which he has a prostetic leg but he wanted to swim before putting on
title: When to babies take centre stage

body: This is a well respected elephant orphanage affiliated with the national park, that cares for as many as 40-50 orphan elephants at any given time. They also help rehabilitate injured elephants that need care. You can visit the center and observe the elephants play and feeding time for about a 20 minute window 3 times a day. The elephants are a joy to watch, they play in the pond and with each other and seem to really enjoy themselves. Once feeding time is over, the caretakers call out to the elephants to let them know to move along and it is amazing to see the elephants listen to the orders and act just by the caretaker’s voices. No chains or hooks or anything other than voices are used to guide the elephants from one area to another. Be sure to visit this center and stay away from Pinnawala (a place that uses chains and only claims to be an orphanage to attract tourists)I also saw a sign while here advertising a program similar to that of the David Sheldrick Wildlife Trust in Kenya where you can foster an orphan elephant and ensure that your donations contribute to your orphan's future.
title: Wonderful experience

body: We visited the elephant transit house early morning with a cost of 500 rupees which all money going to this good cause ! It was very good to see the baby elephants off all different sizes being fed with their powdered milk !!Last about an hour.Very funny and entertaining in parts with some of the antics of these lovely creatures ! Well done to the staff keep up the good work !!
title: Excellent visit

body: Unfortunately, for ETH the 'other' elephant 'sanctuary' gets all the press and was even originally included in my itinerary by my travel agent until I informed them I would NOT go there and asked them to discontinue including it in ANY itinerary. Elephant Transit Home is really the ONLY elephant true sanctuary in Sri Lanka. The other (pinnawala) uses chains and houses ellies for the benefit of the humans - take photos, etc. etc.....and NOT the ellies. It's always so sad to see very young ellies without Mom. I know how close that bond is....but, at least here at ELEPHANT TRASIT HOME they have some chance of growing up and going back to the wild in the adjacent park. The feeding was handled calmly by the humans with some young ellies of course acting up as all young animals are want to do. It was amusing. One orphan has apparently lost a foot and wears a prosthesis. But he was fed separately to eliminate competition and seemed happy enough. His hips are terribly skewed so he must have constant pain...but, again, at least he has a home and friends and certain food coming his way. I applaud the efforts of this ellie sanctuary and gave a generous donation when leaving. They should definitely advertise more where on property to donate. Also, I did not buy from the vendors outside the gates as I wanted ALL of my monies to go directly to ETH.
title: Please support this VERY important elephant sanctuary.

body: This was wonderful, they keep baby elephants until they are ten then release them back to the wild. Cheap and worth a visit, far better than the elephant orphanage
title: Part of a private tour

body: Better experienced during feeding times, which is 09:00 AM, 12:00 Noon and 03:00 PM, you can get a good view of their activities and the interactions with their human caretakers. Brought from the wild (mainly from wild life parks) abandoned or injured baby elephants are well looked after till they can survive in their own and released to their natural habitat.Good experience for the kids as they learn what it takes to nature the baby elephant to the large animal it tends to be and release to the wild so that we may still see these magnificent animals in years to come.The information centre at the site hold much information about the species which is quite useful for education and if your into wildlife.Tickets are reasonable priced, and one should not miss a visit to this place. Totally worth it.
title: A must visit, lot of things to see and learn

body: Please take note this is the only elephant orphanage in Sri Lanka. Outside of wild-life parks also one of the only true sanctuaries for elephants that visitors can freely visit knowing the animals are being treated well and the proceeds are going to elephant conservation and their return to the wild, a good cause. There are many facilities claiming such like the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage and Elephant Freedom Project etc that are nothing of the sort. On the very edge of the wilds near the entrance to and directly bordering the Uda Walawe National Park is Elephant Transit Home.This is a wonderful facility that takes in young elephants in trouble from the wilds and returns them to wild using the most unobtrusive methods possible. The elephants are not trained, they aren't ridden and do not perform tricks for tourists. Instead they are fed up to health and reintroduced to a life in the wild in the quickest safest and kindest way possible avoiding any excessive human contact. It may be a little upsetting to see them being guided with light sticks in and out of the feeding area at times but this minimises contact and the need to train them further than tapping with the sticks.Highly recommended and also by the way endorsed and in part supported by the "Born Free Foundation".We visited during our stay and trip to the Uda Walawe National Park and couldn't have been happier that we did. The entrance fee is very reasonable however a donation on top of the entrance fee would very well received. There is also the possibility to adopt and sponsor a calf.The only thing that saddens us were the sheer numbers of little elephants calves that were in the facility. This is not a good sign and we were left worrying about the consequences behind the numbers of orphaned and injured calves that needed rescuing. Sri Lanka is not a large country but it has a large wild elephant population and they come into contact with people as a result and in many cases this is not a happy meeting. Lives and livelihoods need protecting as do those of the elephants. Many many elephants are killed in these conflicts and many orphans are sadly the result. Finding a happy safe path for both is proving very difficult and you will see evidence of this almost everywhere you go in Sri Lanka.The best time to go to Elephant Transit Home is early in the morning around 9am, this we found at least was the time with the fewest visitors so the the noise and crowds were minimum. Unfortunately they don't always enforce the silence asked for and especially children but certainly not exclusively can make far too much noise. We had arrived at 3pm and it was both busy and noisy so as our hotel wasn't so far and we were self driving we decided to come back the next day. When we did we had it mostly all to ourselves, it was also nice and cool and the elephants were in a very playful mood, there were also a good number of birds around.Whats so nice for the elephants is that the tourist don't get to ride or interact with them at all, they come in get fed milk and play around the water hole area, this happens four times a day 9am, 12noon, 3pm and at 6pm. The rest of the time the babies enjoy the freedom being looked after by a carers in the park itself, here they learn the skills of foraging and living in the wild, being normal elephants.If you've visited any other facilities with captive elephants in Sri Lanka you will immediately notice the difference. The elephants here are alert and playful and have formed friendships with each other. They are learning without pain to be elephants and not slaves to the desires of man. These friendships are very important as they will also be life long making a transition into the wild a lot easier. It's also very cute seeing elephant calves interacting with each other as they are absolutely adorable and you will most certainly fall in love.Visiting Udawalawe National Park itself was also wonderful. Contrary to popular opinion early morning and before dusk are not the best times to visit as everyone goes at these times and so there are far too many jeeps. You need to hire a designated jeep and driver to enter, these can be arranged through your hotel or some way before the gate entrance where you will see them parked along the side of the road. The jeeps chase this or that, usually leopard sightings, when it can literally descend into an absolute chaotic circus which is also not very nice for the wild-life or for natural viewing. The jeeps are open sided and mostly covered so you have shade and a breeze and quite frankly the elephants will be around in numbers what ever time you go especially if the grass is lush and green after good rains. Take a nice frozen drink or even a flask of tea and a sarnwich or two! Enjoy, ask your driver to stop frequently under trees to rest and take in the scenery and atmosphere, sounds etc, it's then that you see the best sightings, the big stuff can wait.ETH is definitely worth it and your patronage and we can only hope in the future there will be less need for an orphanage, but still very relieved there is one.
title: The real Sri Lankan Elephant Orphanage

body: It was wonderful to see around 40 baby elephants ages up to 5 years running across the feeding paddock to get their milk and food. Seeing them interact with each other and play in the pond was amazing. And it's great that this is saving elephant lives. However the signs telling us to keep silent in Sinhalese and English were very much ignored by locals and tourists alike. The signs certainly need to be in German and French (as I guess they were unable to read the signs and were yapping loudly all the way through). And the staff need to tell people to shut up, it really ruined the ambience and made it hard to hear the elephants, it's not fair on the elephants too.
title: Brilliant but they need to enforce the silence rule

body: Memories to treasure. Visit at feeding times x3 daily to see the elephants all come for their milk and a wallow in the pool. Easy to see from a viewing platform and take photos.So reassuring to see the elephant welfare,the aim is to release them in to the park when they are able to cope. The elephants are well cared for no evidence of any cruelty, any funds help with the continuing work of this valuable cause.
title: Do not miss this!

body: Fantastic experience to watch the elephant being fed and enjoying themselves in a natural environment. This is the only sanctuary endorsed by Born Free where elephants are treated with respect and not harmed. Money paid goes back into the elephants re-homing. Incredible program.
title: Mind blowing!!

body: We went to the ETH for the 0900 feeding time, and found it an enchanting experience. Although visitors are corralled onto a viewing platform and cannot get close to the elephants, it was wonderful to see around 40 animals of all sizes being fed with milk and frolicking in a pool. One baby even tried his luck by attempting to go round twice!One larger elephant had an artificial foot - the result we were told of a landmine - and appeared very well cared for.Elephants are the ETH are often orphans, and the home aims to ready them for re-entry into the adjacent Uda Walaew National Park.
title: Charming experience at a worthwhile enterprise

body: There is no commercialism to this venue. It simply feels like an organisation providing support to orphan elephants who otherwise have no other option. We liked the small education centre and found that very informative.The joy is that even from a distance (you watch from a viewing platform) you can see the personality of some of the babies. The cheeky ones, the quieter ones as well as those who have taken on more maternal roles for other little ones.It's a pleasure to visit and it made the trip for our children. You can offer a donation but ensure you take it to the office and they will provide a receipt - it goes towards much needed milk powder. Great work and a privilege to watch and if you're in the area definitely worth a visit.
title: Brilliant work being done!

body: This was my favourite trip in Sri Lanka. It was a very simple uncommercial organisation. The elephants are taken in,made better and then released back to the wild. We saw so many elephants and had such a good view of them
title: A fabulously special trip

body: This was probably one of the cutest activity of all times. Seeing the babies come through to get fed one by one, running as quick as possible; its just great. The views are very good from the balcony amd you can get good pictures. As an elephant lover I would have loved the opportunity to feed a baby but it was very strictly made clear that this couldn't be done, which i understood following the nature of this transit home.
title: So many babies, you want to take them home!

body: Take an hour to watch baby elephants get fed and play. 500Rs entry fee helps to buy milk for the elephants. They have had an excellent rate of elephants rejoining herds.
title: Excellent rehabilitation rate

body: Make sure you be there for one of the feeding times, apart from these feeding sessions, there is not that much to see.Entrance is quite cheap.Seeing the feeding is great!
title: must see

body: Incredible experience. The elephants appear really well looked after. They're rehabilitated and released into the wild when they're ready, then tracked to see how they settle. There is a 500 LKR entrance fee and four feeding times a day (9am, 12pm, 3pm & 6pm). There are some stalls outside selling snacks and elephant themed gifts, but you could wait until you're inside and buy gifts from the shop as this goes back to the orphanage. Get in line 20 mins before to buy your ticket and secure yourself a good viewing spot. Highly, highly recommend! Visit the information centre to learn about the elephants
title: Amazing

body: A wonderful place to visit. We targeted the mid day feed, happen every 3 hours- and had a lovely hour or so watching the variety of young elephants being fed and then relaxing by the pool!This place does wonderful work - well managed and with a helpful 'museum'/ info centre.
title: Great feeding experience

body: Won't ever forget this. It was wonderful. It costs next to nothing to get in and at 12 o' clock you can watch the young calves coming for their milk, to play in the water and to have fun. It was magical watching these animals interact with each other. A must visit if at all possible.
title: Wonderful experience

body: This is not worth the detour. No explanation , just the feeding of the different elephants. Now if you are a great fan of elephants, than it might be OK.But in view of the distance between you and the animals it feels like being in a zoo. So why go there?
title: Just a few minutes show

body: If you're in Sri Lanka this is the elephant "orphanage" to visit - it's doing a great job and putting its orphaned elephants back into the wild. If you see a radio collared elephant in the nearby National Park - it's come from here. You stand on a raised platform and view the elephants coming into a large area where the youngsters are fed milk. Then they wander closer to you. Don't expect to be too close - this place is not a zoo. There is a good education area.
title: Its doing a great job

body: This is on the edge of the Udawalawe Safari park and is a Government sponsored facility. The baby elephants are in the park except for feeding time which is four times a day. You watch from a balcony and have good views. From what we could tell from our research this was the best place to go for this. Although in fact we had seen many babies on our safaris.
title: A wonderful visit to see the baby elephants being fed

body: Takes about 1h to see the elephant being ved and to check out the information centre and read facts about elephants.There was a good distance between the public and elephants. Adorable to see how the babys drink milk and how the herd takes a bath before they return to their own part of the park. The caretakers where humain to the animals.A nice surprise!
title: Good cause and nice visit

body: Orphan baby elephants were fed with milk. Around 30 small elephants are raised and released after some years. Good projects and nice to see the small elephants being fed the milk.
title: Always nice to see

body: We visited the home around lunchtime, the elephants were very amusing and always wanted more food, the kids loved seeing them rolling round in the mud. They must have about 50 elephants here.
title: Very entertaining

body: It is an interesting moment to see when they feed all the elephants. You will be amaze to watch them and how they behave.
title: Feeding time

body: As others have said, what could be cuter than watching baby elephants charging towards a feeding station to receive their milk?! It was great to see their personalities come out, some shy, some greedy and some downright cheeky! We didn't like seeing the mahout use the cane on some of the elephants. Not sure if it hurts the elephants but they didn't seem to like it. Visitor centre is very small. The transit home is not expensive and well worth the price.
title: Well worth a visit

body: We visited this after going on the safari at Underwalawe National Park. At first all seemed good and well organised and I was slightly taken back , as they would let so many in at a time as so there wasn't a free for all. But there was one greedy baby elephant who would try his luck, which was very entertaining. Then they let more elephants in which was lead by a Mahut with a very small elephant , and this is where it didn't sit right with me. The Mahut started whipping the older greedy one to make him move out of the way. I understand that there has to be rules and obviously some kind of safety around them, but this man just kept hitting this elephant and even putting his weight behind the stick and actually seemed to enjoy whipping him. At that point I left the grounds as I didn't want to see any more. In principle this Transit home works but the actions of this man on that day made me want to cry. I will not recommend this attraction to any one. Just go to the national park there.
title: Not that different from the other elephant homes around.

body: We visited this camp with friends after visiting Udawalawe National Park. It is only about ten minutes drive from the park. We arrived at feeding time, 12 noon and there must have been over a hundred people, including school parties waiting. The young elephants were let in a few at a time and they knew the routine. Go to the feeding station where they receive a pipe and funnel which is filled with milk. When it's gone its time to move away and allow the next one in. Sometimes they try for more and there is a man making sure it doesn't happen. There were one or two scuffles but on the whole they all knew what to do. Once they had had their milk they could got to the water to wallow or play or to the jack fruit branches which had been cut for them and eat. Some of the smaller ones kept us amused and a land monitor came by very close as well. The whole routine lasted about twenty minutes and was over all too soon. On the way out our guide steered us towards a pair of Scops owls in a tree near the entrance - bonus!
title: Very worthwhile work

body: If you are more interested in conservation than in elephant tourism, this is the place for you! We were booked to go to the orphanage, but I did some research, which said that it is a commercial enterprise where the elephants are not being rescued. The ETH on the other hand is a pure conservation site! They feed the babies every three hours from 6am, it is cheap to get in, and all the money goes to helping the elephants. It was also the cutest thing I have ever seen! Elephants queuing to get their feed, then running over with their trunks up ready. Seriously, if you want cute, and you are into conservation, you definitely have to go!
title: Made me cry it was so cute!
Cuteness Overload
body: Our 13 year olds description of ETH. This is where orphaned elephants are housed until they are 5 and can be returned to the wild. This means that about 40 elephants ranging from 6 months to 5 years can be seen being fed milk in tubes every 3 hours. It is amazing to watch as they approach the feeding area in little groups and greedily drink their allotted milk. Watch as the cheeky ones try to go for more while others wrestle each other with their trunks. The centre relies on the 500 rupees paid by visitors for funding so try to visit if you are in the area, you will not be disappointed.

title: feeding time was wounderful
body: their were lot of baby elephants whom they bring to feed, you must visit during the feed times of 6am 9am 12noon 3pm and 6pm. entry ticket for local is Rs 20/- and you can make donations for milk which is provided to elephants. it was a nice Experience. enjoyed a lot.

title: Worth the time
body: We went one morning to the elephant orphanage at feeding time which is every three hours. It was quite a quick tour lasting only thirty minutes. It was nice to see the elephants being looked after and feeding as some of them had physical disabilities. The only bad point was we should have been told to arrive earlier before the feeding times to see the elephants for a little longer.

title: great if you don't have time for a safari
body: get there for feeding time and see elephants of all ages get fed. Really nice to see, especially if you don't have time for a safari, or if you were unlucky enough to not see any elephants outside in the open.

title: A must visit
body: This is a very unique place to visit. The baby elephants come from the forest for their milk which is absolutely adorable. 30 baby elephants. So nice it's a must visit destination.

title: Very Busy
body: We visited following a safari in the nearby national park. There were lots of young elephants being cared for. However, when we visited it was feeding time and it was incredibly busy with tourists meaning most people could not see any of the animals.

title: Orphan elephants
body: Great to see the care of these elephants before they are released into the wild.Human contact is kept to a minimum so that these ophans can be released successfully

title: Worth to visit
body: Elephant Transit Home (ETH) is situated very close to Udawalawe National park. ETH feedings times are 06 AM , 09 AM, 12 AM , 03 PM & 06 PM.Best thing is tourists cant touch or feed the elephants.When Elephants are getting matured they will release to the National parks.Highly recommend to visit if you have children... .

title: Amazing experience!
body: Such a phenomenal experience!Feed times are 9am, 12am, 3pm and 6pm.Follow directions for the district hospital and then it's about 15 metres further along on the right (as you walk from the main road).Only 500lkr ppSo worth a visit!

title: Fantastic
body: This place was a real surprise on our visit to Uda Walawe. We organised a trip to the park and after a 3 hour drive we pulled up at this place. We were told it was an elephant feeding station for baby elephants. What more can I say? How cute are baby elephants and how grumpy can they get when they are told they get no more milk?! LOL. Go and see for yourself.It is a real treat to watch this before a safari Highly recommended!
